articles.title: A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
articles.body:
“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.
A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.
By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.
Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.
“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”
But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.
The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.
It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.
On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”
Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.
The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.
Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.
The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.
Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.
On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.
Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $111 million of Nvidia shares in the largest-ever first half-hour of opening for the stock, Bloomberg reported, citing Vanda Research.
They might be onto something.
Nvidia’s average price target is $232.59, with the lowest estimate at $130 and the highest at $350, according to an analysis of analyst projections over the last three months by Google Finance.
Nearly two-thirds of those analysts issued a “Buy” rating for Nvidia in the last three months. Of those, all 30 reiterated that rating post-earnings.
The stock closed at $145.98 on Thursday, a new 52-week low.
Then again, numbers are the core basis for stock market ratings, and numbers may not be Nvidia’s problem right now. It’s everything else — the leadership vacuum, upcoming congressional testimony, regulatory uncertainty, broader questions about neocloud customer financing and sales to China — that will continue to impact the stock in the coming weeks.

articles.title: AI Came for the Coders. Understanding Why Tells Us Who's Next
articles.body:
I used to joke that I got my degree in poetry instead of computer engineering so that, in case this computing fad went south, I would have something to fall back on. Thanks to AI, it’s barely a joke anymore.
Software engineering, where I’ve spent a good part of the last 25 years of my career, is undergoing a crisis of faith. True believers in the beauty of hand-written code have had it wrested from them. Those who like solving problems and making things with technology, code or no, have been given new toys to play with and tools to master.
I liken it to carpentry from the 19th century onward, when jack planes, chisels and hand saws gave way to power sanders, routers, and table saws. The industry scaled, and now ordinary people can afford decent furniture. But there was another cost.
The straightforward nature of physical automation
If you were happy to become a machine operator instead of a craftsman, you were in business. However, if you fell in love with thin ribbons of wood from a hand plane catching the light, about the only remaining way to make a living now is by filming your craft and becoming an influencer for nostalgic hobbyists.
We embraced the automation of manual labour as it led to benefits for many, in affordable goods and free time. We devalued craftsmanship in the bargain. Working at a desk became more respected than making a desk. But when the work of smart coders gets rocked this hard, fear ripples through the desk worker world. If such intellectual work is vulnerable, then what, and who, is next?
A comforting but wrong answer is that the “human” stuff is safe, and coding is technical. A much better way to understand what human skills will endure AI automation is to look at a principle as old as machine learning, and one that goes a long way toward explaining what can and cannot be automated by AI. It hasn’t changed since the 50s, and is unlikely to be broken anytime soon. It is easy enough to understand, yet what it predicts can be counterintuitive.
So many wrong assumptions, and so much baseless fear-mongering, stem from misunderstanding the nature of AI automation’s natural trajectory.
The counterintuitive nature of digital automation
In aid of my language studies, I recently created a clone of my voice to help with pronunciation. It took a few hours and about $5 of computing credits to retrain a free open-source model, which now runs locally on my MacBook, entirely within my control. I used it to record one of my AI explainer videos, and played it for my wife, a professional musician with a great sensitivity to voice, who has lived with me for nearly 25 years.
She couldn’t tell it wasn’t me.
Making art, writing poems and songs, and recognising the face or voice of a loved one feel like inherently human activities. Some of it, like facial recognition, has gone the way computer scientist Larry Tesler predicted: “Intelligence is whatever machines haven’t done yet”. The term “intelligent” didn’t stick to it for long. It has just become a part of everyday life.
The ones that feel most like “us”, though, such as art, writing, speaking, and even code, have shaken our sense of identity when done by a machine. Here the AI label stuck fast. Machines doing work we identify with causes us to project our self-image of intelligence onto them as well.
Yet AI can also appear incredibly dumb. Researchers who study AI at work have a name for the lopsided progress of AI across disciplines: the jagged frontier.1 It turns out the line between what the machines do well and what they do badly runs nowhere near the line between what we find hard and what we find easy.
The frontier only looks ragged because we are measuring it by how “human” the work feels, which means some disciplines and even industries won’t “just catch up” to the outer edge anytime soon.
The truth is, speech synthesis and everything else we either take for granted or fear will bring about our obsolescence all conform to the laws of what AI can automate well. These are rules that follow from how machines “learn”, which is also a purely anthropomorphic metaphor.
Understanding what can be automated
The first AI programmes of the 1950s were specified with rules of reasoning written by hand. The ones that learned arrived in the same decade, among them a programme at IBM that improved at draughts by playing against earlier versions of itself.2 Learning needs something more than just design; it needs a way to keep score. This is why AI plays games so well, eventually surpassing us in finding the best way to win.
AI researcher Jason Wei coined “verifier’s law”: the easier a task is to check, the easier it is to train AI to do it. Andrej Karpathy distinguishes the old way of doing software as what you can specify and the new way as what you can verify.3 A digital recording of a voice, it turns out, is easy to check, and easy to verify against the reference voice being cloned.
For simplicity, I have bundled all of the elements that Wei and others have identified as necessary for checking and verifying, such as having a right answer, being able to score it reliably, and being able to automate it with sufficient computing power to do it over and over again at high speed, into the term “grading”.
All components are necessary to perform AI automation today. But even as data and computing power become more available, at the end of the day some numerical form of analysis, and some evaluation of “correctness”, are make-or-break factors in what can (ever) be graded.
Grading, however, is only part of what predicts AI automation. The other part is value, and our agreement on what valuable means. Plotting work along these two dimensions gives us four boxes to consider.
Software is among the most-graded work humans have ever produced. It compiles or it doesn’t, the tests pass or they fail, and the automated testing takes seconds on ordinary machines. As long as it’s fit for purpose, nobody disputes that working software is worth having, which puts code in the top-right box. My cloned voice sits beside it. It either passes the wife test or it doesn’t.
Yet, as I have said before, there will never be a compiler that can check for bugs in your poem. You can clone a poet’s style, and follow all conventions of form just right. But poetry’s greatest trick is evading mediocrity, which is precisely what endless iterations of numerical comparison and adjustment converge upon. Form and style can be graded; whether the poem is any good cannot. That puts poetry in the bottom-right box. I did a whole talk on it, if you want to hear more.
From the standpoint of society, parenting is perhaps the most important job in the world. Grading it automatically (or at all) seems absurd, not least of all because it can take years, even generations, to see the results, which are themselves often easy to recognise but hard to quantify. It sits top left, high in value but beyond grading.
The last box holds work that can be neither graded nor valuated objectively. Our carpenters who became hobbyist woodworkers got put in this box by the physical machinery of automation, yet now remain immune to digital automation as a result. Like poetry, the value of the product is a matter of taste, and taste diverges, eluding quantification.
Predicting what will be automated
Beyond coding, the automation of art and writing feels like the solution to a “problem” that almost nobody wanted to be solved.4 So much of what has been automated most of us lament, and so much of what has not been automated we begrudge. This is because the possibilities of AI automation do not follow our wishes, but follow the principles of automated grading versus objective value outlined above. It also doesn’t matter how “human” it feels: if it scores high on both, it’s possible. This doesn’t make it probable, however. It just shows us where to rule out the impossible.
What makes it probable is market incentive. This is different from being able to agree on objective value. This is about capitalism, and the dream of owning the means of production not only for labour, but for knowledge work. For a few decades, a creative with a laptop owned their own means of production, which is more than any mill hand ever could. AI that cranks out marketing imagery on demand hands those means back to whoever pays for the subscription, with only a small amount of remaining work required to publish it and finish the job.
Commercial art and writing are in this category. A brief and a paying client supply value agreement, and steady income, that fine art lacks. AI is automating creative commercial work, which means that artists will find it harder to make a living using the same skills as their fine art or literary practice.
I must point out, though, that rarely throughout history has anyone who wants to make a living in fine arts been able to do so easily. Van Gogh lived on an allowance from his brother, and a great many famous artists lived on their inheritance. The nepo-baby is a timeless tradition.
For the last century or so, there were also side-hustles and day jobs: Warhol drew shoe advertisements, Hopper illustrated magazines, Rushdie wrote advertising copy, and Hemingway and Orwell worked as journalists. Practicing art-making commercially to hone skills, and to cover the rent while doing so, is what is really under threat in the AI age.
My own qualitative estimate of how artists and writers have lived without a second profession.5
For most illustrators, copywriters, and translators, of course, the commercial work was never a rehearsal for something higher. It was the job. In a Society of Authors survey, a quarter of illustrators and over a third of translators said they had already lost work to generative AI.6 For them, the option on offer is, like the carpenters of old, to become a machine operator.
Re-skilling for the AI age
In knowledge work, AI produces deliverables; people achieve outcomes. A deliverable is a thing you can hand over: the report, the code, the slide deck, the campaign image. An outcome is what the thing was for in the first place, such as a presentation you give to the board or a sales deal you close. It only happens when other people agree, adopt, and follow through with complex social interactions.
Many deliverables can be graded, which is why AI keeps getting better at those that can. Parenting, by contrast, is a complex set of outcomes, each unarguably valuable yet all ungradeable.
Then there is the question of accountability. When things go wrong, a model has no neck to choke. However, if you get fired for work you did with AI, your replacement will sit in the same office chair and use the same AI subscription plan.
Capitalism keeps people answerable with an existential threat: if you don’t work, you don’t eat. It operates a long way below a craftsman’s pride in their work. But it operates, like a machine. Markets, after all, have their own intelligence to them.
In light of these forces at work, everything outside of what can and will be automated should be the focus of our modern skilling, in both institutional and corporate education. Equally important is to understand how to use AI automations to enhance the value of the outcomes we achieve, and indeed the lives we lead.
For an individual, that means a few good habits: decide what the outcome is before requesting the deliverables; check what comes back as though your name were on it (because it will be!); stay close enough to the work that you can verify it is both correct and fit for purpose. I have developed these research-led practices into a method called DRIVE.
School grading teaches us everything can be measured, which is why we’re terrified of failing. Objective measures make schooling scalable, and therefore readily available (like furniture), but at the expense of the intangibles now most valuable in the AI era: personal story, big-picture creative thinking, wise judgment, unshakeable ethics, and the ability to struggle in order to learn. I made the case for struggle in particular in Knowing the Answer Was Never the Point.
Collectively, the work is to stop valuing ourselves only in relation to what can be graded. Schools must spend less time on grades as a proxy for having learned, and more time on learning how to learn and think in itself. Employers must keep taking on beginners, and treating them like future leaders, lest they have none to choose from in the next decade.7 Those who gain most from AI automation must share what they discover. Learning from one another about AI, ourselves, and our values can give us back the feeling of being a team.
Hope? Really?
Nearly all anti-AI arguments I have come across use AI as a flashpoint for lamenting the polarisation of wealth, and the capture of knowledge work. The grievance is real; the technology is where it shows most sharply, because it hits us where it hurts, in our intellectual identity.
As a coder and creative, I’ve been gut-punched twice; you would think I’d be anything but hopeful about the future. My optimism comes from understanding what AI can and cannot automate, where beyond the tool itself late capitalism has a part in all this mess, and of necessity: my nephews will inherit an AI-native world. I want to do everything I can to be a force for good in bridging us into a future where we are appropriately refocused on using AI intelligently, safely, and well for the benefit of all.
Meanwhile the poetry stays where it has always belonged, in my back pocket.
- Fabrizio Dell’Acqua and colleagues, Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, Organization Science 37(2), first circulated in 2023: a field experiment with 758 consultants at Boston Consulting Group. ↩︎
- The designed programme was Logic Theorist (Newell, Shaw, and Simon, 1956). The one that learned was Arthur Samuel’s, described in “Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers” (1959), the paper that popularised the term machine learning. ↩︎
- Jason Wei, Asymmetry of verification and verifier’s rule (2025). Andrej Karpathy, Verifiability (2025). ↩︎
- Stanford’s WORKBank audit asked 1,500 workers about 844 tasks across 104 occupations between January and May 2025. Workers welcomed automation on 46.1% of those tasks overall, and on 17.1% in arts, design, and media. These are shares of tasks, not of people. ↩︎
- The chart is informed guesswork throughout, checked against surveys only for its last two decades. Read it for its shape. The Church gave way to secular patrons, patrons to the open market, and the market to commercial creative work, shown in orange, which by my estimate has carried art practice for about 140 years. Two surveys sit behind its right-hand edge. Arts Council England’s Livelihoods of Visual Artists (2018) asked 2,007 artists in March 2016 about their income in 2015: 90% said their art practice did not earn them enough to live on, and almost seven in ten had another job. The UK authors’ earnings survey found the share of professional authors living on writing alone fell from 40% in 2006 to 19% in 2022. ↩︎
- Society of Authors survey, January 2024, 787 responses: 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators. A separate study of about 1.4 million freelance job posts found that writing and coding posts fell 21% against manual-skill posts in the eight months after ChatGPT launched, and image-creation posts fell 17% (Demirci, Hannane, and Zhu, Management Science, 2025). ↩︎
- Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine?, August 2026 revision, from US payroll records to June 2026. Employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in the occupations most exposed to AI runs about 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with their peers in less exposed work, mostly because fewer are being hired. The authors stress that this is a pattern in the data and does not prove AI caused it. ↩︎

articles.title: Anthropic starts trading on Wall Street
articles.body:
Anthropic has officially gone public. It began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT” at $111.50 per share, up from its initial $83 per share price that put company’s value at around $1.5 trillion.
Anthropic starts trading on Wall Street
Anthropic began trading at $111.50 per share.
Anthropic began trading at $111.50 per share.
The listing comes nearly a month after Anthropic revealed its plans to go public. In its lengthy S-1 filing, the AI company reported recording an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of this year, most of which comes from an accounting charge that doesn’t reflect its business, along with $16.3 billion in revenue. The filing outlines plans that Anthropic says will help it develop AI for the benefit of humanity, which includes a governance structure that keeps control of the company in the hands of the founders, rather than the shareholders.
While speaking ahead of Anthropic’s debut at the Nasdaq, CEO Dario Amodei highlighted his stance on AI safety. “To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei said, according to Reuters. “We will not bend to either business nor political pressure.”
Anthropic’s S-1 filing also listed possible “catastrophic” risks associated with its AI models, including “self-preserving behaviors” like resisting attempts to shut them down. It also warns potential shareholders that its AI models “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that can harm Anthropic.
Anthropic recently revealed that, like rival OpenAI, it has experienced incidents of AI agents escaping their testing environment and hacking third-party organizations. In September, Amodei proposed a plan to slow down the training and development of AI in response to the wave of rogue AI cyberattacks. As part of that plan, it gave safety evaluators at METR “employee-like access” to its internal systems, who found that the company is using AI to accelerate its research and development.

articles.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
articles.body:
Three people with inoperable pancreatic cancer had stable disease after receiving an experimental virus treatment in a University of Minnesota Phase I trial. The university first reported the findings in June 2026. In a fall follow-up, it said one participant had reached 15 months of disease control.
The treatment uses a genetically engineered adenovirus injected into a tumor. It aims to enter malignant cells, replicate within them, and destroy them, potentially making the cancer easier for the immune system to recognize.
“Halted” in this setting refers to the reported control of disease during follow-up. It should not be read as proof that every cancer cell was eliminated, that tumors disappeared or that the treatment has been shown to extend survival compared with standard care.
The scientific interest is substantial: a biological agent that can multiply inside its target offers a different way to attack a difficult cancer. The clinical question is whether that mechanism can deliver a durable benefit without unacceptable harm.
The latest report adds follow-up, not a final verdict
The university’s Fall 2026 account says the three people in the lowest dose group had inoperable tumors and had each survived beyond six months. It reports 15 months of disease control for one participant and describes higher dose testing as the next step.
Those observations are meaningful for the people involved. They are also preliminary institutional reporting, without the detailed patient timelines, imaging assessments and adverse event tables that a full clinical publication would provide.
It is not possible to turn three cases into a dependable success rate. The duration of control, earlier treatments, tumor characteristics and the way participants were selected all influence how a result should be interpreted.
Comparing these individuals with a broad survival statistic would not establish a treatment effect. A valid comparison needs patients with sufficiently similar disease, previous care and health status, assessed from the same starting point.
The six-month and 15-month figures describe different outcomes. The first tells us the three participants were alive beyond a given point. The second describes the time during which one participant’s disease was reported under control. A person can live well beyond the point at which a cancer starts to grow again, so one measure cannot stand in for the other.
A full account would also identify when the clock started for each measure. Fifteen months counted from diagnosis, enrollment or the injection would describe different periods. Showing those dates alongside scan results and any other treatments would let readers see whether the three participants followed similar courses.
The trial is designed to answer safety and dosing questions
The registered study, NCT06693986, investigates RGDCRAdCOX2F, a modified conditionally replicative adenovirus. Its primary objective is to establish a maximally tolerated dose through direct tumor injection.
A dose escalation study increases exposure in a structured way while monitoring toxicity. The purpose is to identify a dose that can reasonably be taken forward, rather than assuming that the highest possible amount must be the most useful.
The National Cancer Institute record lists preliminary clinical activity as a secondary objective. Separate biological objectives examine effects in the tumor and immune responses generated against the virus.
That distinction helps explain the status of the findings. Researchers can observe disease control while testing safety, but the trial’s first task is not the same as demonstrating superiority over an established treatment.
The public outline describes an injection on day one, imaging and tissue sampling, and collection of blood, urine and saliva. Follow up is scheduled every three months for one year after study treatment.
Some participants may undergo surgery under the protocol; others undergo biopsy and endoscopic ultrasound assessments. These procedures allow investigators to learn about the treated tissue as well as observe what happens on scans.
For patients, the safety question includes both the experimental treatment and the procedure used to deliver it. A full results report would document the severity and duration of problems, whether they required hospitalization or delayed other care, and whether the investigators linked them to the injection procedure, the treatment itself or the underlying cancer. The university’s follow-up does not provide a breakdown of those outcomes.
Early trials also give researchers a chance to learn whether an intervention can fit into a patient’s care. An injection may take place on a single day, but the surrounding visits, scans and follow-up tests can stretch over months. If the approach advances, the time patients spend undergoing tests and recovering from procedures will be part of assessing its value.
Why this is a particular pancreatic cancer population
The trial concerns pancreatic adenocarcinoma confined to the pancreas and regional lymph nodes. Disease extending beyond the regional lymph nodes is excluded in the public eligibility criteria.
Locally advanced cancer and cancer that has spread to distant organs present different treatment problems. A result after injecting one localized tumor cannot establish control of metastatic deposits throughout the body.
Participants must also be able to undergo endoscopy, and the tumor must be accessible by ultrasound guided procedures. People for whom biopsy is unsafe or infeasible are excluded.
The protocol permits one prior line of therapy, with a waiting period before injection. It sets criteria for organ function, blood counts and general physical condition and excludes several conditions that could complicate safety.
These requirements protect participants and make the experiment interpretable. They also mean the first treated patients are a selected group, rather than a representative sample of everyone diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.
The eligibility rules should be understood as features of this particular research protocol. They are not a general guide to deciding which treatment an individual patient should receive.
Where the trial fits into pancreatic cancer care
For locally advanced pancreatic cancer, the National Cancer Institute’s treatment review identifies chemotherapy as the main treatment. Some patients may receive radiation with chemotherapy, and a smaller group can be reconsidered for surgery after treatment. Care can also include relief of complications such as a blocked bile duct. These decisions depend on the tumor’s location and the patient’s overall condition.
A pancreatic tumor that involves major blood vessels can be difficult to remove safely even when scans show no distant spread. After treatment, a multidisciplinary team can reassess where the tumor sits in relation to those vessels and look for signs that cancer has appeared elsewhere. The size of the tumor is one part of that assessment.
Earlier research illustrates why control of a tumor and longer survival deserve separate measurements. In the randomized LAP07 trial, people whose locally advanced cancer was controlled after initial chemotherapy were assigned to further chemotherapy or to chemoradiotherapy. Chemoradiotherapy reduced local progression, while the study found no significant difference in overall survival between those groups. LAP07 investigated a different treatment, but it shows why later virus trials would need to track both outcomes.
If the Minnesota team eventually tests whether the injection can make an inoperable cancer removable, a key result would be how many participants actually underwent surgery. Researchers would also want to know whether the removed tissue had clear margins, how patients recovered and whether the cancer returned. Those outcomes would put an encouraging scan in clinical context.
How an adenovirus becomes a therapeutic tool
An oncolytic virus is a virus investigated or used for its ability to infect and destroy cancer cells. “Oncolysis” describes the breaking apart of those cells, but reaching them selectively is a major part of the engineering challenge.
The trial description explains that pancreatic cancer cells can be relatively resistant to ordinary adenoviral infection because they have insufficient levels of the usual cellular entry receptor. Modifying viral targeting is intended to help overcome that obstacle.
Entry and replication are separate problems. An engineered virus needs to gain access to the cancer cell, then reproduce under conditions that favor the tumor over healthy tissue.
A 2024 review by Shivani Thoidingjam and colleagues in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences explains how tumor selective promoters and other genetic modifications can restrict replication or improve immune stimulation. These design choices differ between viral products.
Once a susceptible cancer cell is infected, the virus uses the cell’s machinery to make additional viral particles. Destruction of that cell can release particles that infect neighboring cells, potentially extending the local effect.
This mechanism is a scientific rationale, not a guarantee that every tumor cell will be reached. Distribution through a real tumor, variation among cells and the patient’s antiviral defenses can limit the process.
A pancreatic tumor has defenses beyond the cancer cells
Pancreatic cancers often contain dense fibrous supporting tissue, known as a desmoplastic stroma. This environment can influence the movement of treatments and the behavior of immune cells.
The 2024 review describes the extracellular matrix as one barrier to effective treatment. Cancer associated fibroblasts, immune cells and signaling molecules also contribute to the tumor’s surrounding ecosystem.
Injecting a treatment into a tumor addresses one delivery challenge: it places the agent near the intended target. It does not automatically ensure uniform spread through all parts of that tumor.
Researchers are therefore investigating several additional strategies. Some experimental viruses carry genes intended to alter the surrounding matrix; others deliver immune stimulating molecules or are combined with different therapies.
Those examples help explain the wider research landscape. They should not be assumed to describe modifications present in RGDCRAdCOX2F unless the product’s own documentation establishes them.
The distinction is especially important in this field because many different agents are called “virus therapy.” Adenoviruses, reoviruses, herpes viruses and vaccinia based products have different biological properties and clinical evidence.
The immune response can help and hinder
Destroying a cancer cell releases material that immune cells may recognize, including tumor antigens. In principle, that can help initiate or strengthen an immune response against the malignancy.
The National Cancer Institute’s explanation of oncolytic virus therapy describes this dual ambition: direct tumor destruction and stimulation of antitumor immunity. It is one reason investigators explore combinations with immunotherapies.
But the immune system also fights the virus. An antiviral response can remove viral particles before they have infected enough cancer cells, creating a tension between controlling infection and maintaining the intended treatment effect.
A strong response against the virus is not necessarily a strong response against the cancer. The registered Minnesota trial includes immune measurements precisely because the relationship needs to be studied rather than assumed.
Future tissue and blood analyses could help determine whether the virus reaches its target and whether relevant immune changes follow. Those measurements would complement clinical outcomes without replacing them.
Other trials show why results must remain product specific
Earlier pancreatic cancer studies established that endoscopic injection of biological agents into tumors was feasible. The 2024 review discusses ONYX-015 experiments, including a study in 21 people that combined later injections with gemcitabine.
Feasibility is an important milestone, but it does not mean all subsequent viruses will have the same safety profile or effectiveness. Genetic changes, dosing, delivery schedules and background chemotherapy can all alter outcomes.
The same review describes a randomized Phase II study of pelareorep with carboplatin and paclitaxel that did not improve progression free survival compared with chemotherapy alone. That is a reminder that a plausible biological mechanism does not always translate into a measurable clinical advantage.
Other early combination studies reported disease control or tumor responses, but many were small and lacked randomized comparisons. Their findings are useful for developing hypotheses and designing later experiments, not for ranking treatments across unrelated patient groups.
The Minnesota observations belong to this developing field. They neither prove that oncolytic viruses as a class work against pancreatic cancer nor lose their value because another product failed in a different setting.
A separate Phase I pancreatic cancer study in The Oncologist evaluated talimogene laherparepvec, commonly called T-VEC. Four of nine patients had stable disease, and the study recorded no complete or partial tumor responses. The participants had previously treated advanced cancer, and T-VEC is a different virus from the one used in Minnesota.
That study is a useful example of what a peer-reviewed report can show. The authors published both the scan outcomes and complications, including two infections they attributed to the injection procedure. With those details, readers can weigh a finding of stable disease alongside the practical risks of reaching a pancreatic tumor.
What disease control can and cannot tell us
A tumor can remain approximately unchanged over an assessment interval without disappearing. Stable disease is therefore different from a complete response, and both differ from a demonstrated improvement in survival.
The length of the interval is central. Short term stability and control lasting many months carry different implications, which is why patient level timelines are so valuable in early research.
Investigators also need to distinguish changes in tumor size from symptoms and daily functioning. A scan can provide one measure of disease while a patient’s experience supplies another.
For a useful clinical assessment, reports should make the denominator clear: how many people enrolled, received treatment, completed assessments and remained under follow up. Missing data and withdrawals are part of the evidence, rather than details to omit.
The available university account does not provide that full accounting. Its positive observations justify attention, while the registered protocol identifies the questions the researchers are still working to answer.
Under widely used RECIST 1.1 criteria, researchers measure selected tumors on scans and classify how they change over time. Small changes in size can fall within the stable-disease category. New lesions can also change the overall classification even when the original tumor appears similar. A detailed report of the Minnesota trial would establish which criteria the researchers used and how often they took the measurements.
When researchers publish a larger dataset, a patient timeline can show when treatment began, when growth was first documented and which patients were still being followed when the analysis ended. Someone with an ongoing response at the cutoff has been observed for at least that long, but the eventual duration is still unknown. That distinction matters when one person’s follow-up is much longer than another’s.
Pancreatic tumors can have indistinct edges on scans, a complication the U.S. Food and Drug Administration notes in its guidance on cancer trial endpoints. A full report can explain how the study handled difficult measurements and whether the same imaging approach was used throughout follow-up. It can also show whether a cancer progressed at the treated site, elsewhere in the body or both.
Why treatment combinations are an active research direction
The rationale for combining an oncolytic virus with another therapy is that each might address a different obstacle. A virus could expose tumor material to immune cells while another agent reduces an inhibitory signal.
Chemotherapy can affect tumor cells and immune populations, and treatment timing may influence how well a virus replicates. Combinations therefore require experimental testing; adding two promising agents does not guarantee a better result.
They can also make interpretation harder. If patients receive several treatments together, a response cannot automatically be attributed to the virus, and adverse events may have more than one possible cause.
Trials need to assess the complete regimen, including its practical burden. Repeated procedures, hospital assessments and recovery time matter alongside tumor measurements when judging whether a treatment offers a useful benefit.
A later comparative study could ask whether adding the injection to an established treatment leads to better outcomes than the same treatment alone. Using the same schedule for scans and recording treatment given after progression would make the groups easier to compare. If the study is large enough, researchers could also examine whether the effect differs according to previous therapy or the extent of local disease.
Progression-free survival, overall survival and quality of life would each answer different questions. A patient might value a longer period before the next round of treatment, fewer symptoms or more time at home. Measuring those outcomes alongside tumor size would help establish whether a change visible on scans translates into a benefit patients can feel.
The distinction between survival measures is straightforward. Overall survival tracks how long people live from a defined starting point. Progression-free survival tracks how long they remain alive without the cancer worsening under the trial’s criteria. An injection delivered at one site could affect growth there while cancer still appears elsewhere. Reporting both outcomes would help clarify how far any benefit extends.
The evidence to watch for next
A detailed clinical report would allow independent readers to examine doses, previous treatments, imaging criteria, follow up and side effects for the people treated. It should distinguish observations from explanations proposed to account for them.
For the biological mechanism, evidence of viral activity in tumor tissue would be informative. For clinical value, longer follow up and appropriate comparisons would show whether disease control leads to outcomes that matter to patients.
Any attempt to make an inoperable tumor removable would need to document actual surgery and its results, rather than treating that possibility as an achieved outcome. That is a separate milestone from an initially stable scan.
As enrollment expands, researchers can also learn whether responses vary with tumor characteristics or treatment history. Such differences may help identify the people most likely to benefit, if a benefit is confirmed.
The current result supports continued investigation of an innovative approach to pancreatic cancer. Three reported cases of disease control, including one lasting 15 months in the university’s update, are encouraging observations. Establishing how reliably the treatment works and how it compares with other care remains the work ahead.
Evidence checked November 19, 2026. The trial registration and the National Cancer Institute listing describe the study design. Findings from the first three participants are attributed to the University of Minnesota’s public updates. The 2024 review by Thoidingjam and colleagues provides scientific background on oncolytic viruses.
Featured photograph: National Cancer Institute via Unsplash. This illustrative laboratory image depicts preparation of a different vaccinia based research material, not the adenovirus administered in this trial. No clinical patient images are reproduced.

articles.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic's record IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
articles.body:
Anthropic’s shares have slumped at the start of a second day of trading, as its record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Shares in the frontier AI company, which floated on Thursday, fell by as much as 12% on Friday. They dropped to $85.12, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.
Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.
US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, knocking 2% off the value of the Nasdaq share index, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 10%. The broader S&P 500 share index fell 1%.
Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled -12% to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”
Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.7%. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.
“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Nvidia shares fell by 3%, after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.
Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.7%. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.
“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Nvidia shares fell by 3%, after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.
Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

articles.title: Chile: UFO Sightings by 18th Century Jesuits
articles.body:
Chile: UFO Sightings by 18th Century Jesuits
Source:IIEE Chile
JESUITS IN THE 16TH CENTURY OBSERVED UFOS
The Jesuits pioneered a revolutionary form of Christian socialism with the Guaraní people of Paraguay, challenging the greed of Spanish colonists and Portuguese *bandeirantes*. This atypical system—a model of social organization that flourished in Paraguay among the indigenous population and the Jesuits—was known as "reductions." This took place in the early 17th century (around 1607).
Upon arriving in the region, the religious order encountered the *encomienda* system, under which the Franciscans—in a sense—continued the regime of the Conquest in their dealings with the indigenous people. The Jesuits vehemently opposed this system; while the concept of "reductions" did not originate with them, they utilized this model to counter the *encomienda* system employed by the Franciscans.
In researching this history, we discovered that the archives of the Society of Jesus contain records of extraordinary incidents. They describe countless events revealing that this region—like so many others in South America—is a source of mysteries and enigmas, and that the UFO phenomenon accompanied the Jesuits and indigenous people as they laid the foundations of this new nation. There is a document in these archives that states the following:
"At the San Ignacio de Ipané mission, on August 10, 1631, something strange and luminous was seen streaking across the sky. Between 6 and 7 in the evening, a luminous orb of unusual size was seen rising in the east; it moved not hurriedly, but rather slowly, over the settlement, resembling a full moon. It cast off a great number of sparks toward the east, and upon reaching the western horizon, it flared up with intense light before going dark; then, after the time it takes to recite the Creed, it produced a tremendous blast like a thunderclap."
A few kilometers from this mission lies an area in the Chaco province known as *Campo del Cielo* ("Field of the Sky"—named for the vast number of meteorites that once fell there). While it is natural to consider the possibility of another meteorite, a word-for-word analysis of the document—such as the one conducted by researcher Antonio Las Heras in one of his excellent works on the subject—inevitably raises doubts as to whether the observed object was, in fact, a meteorite.
The object was traveling slowly; the phrase "was seen rising in the east" gives the immediate impression that it "gained altitude." This suggests it may have been one of the earliest recorded instances of a UFO lifting off from the ground in this region, which spans the province of Misiones near the borders with Brazil and Paraguay. Without delving into the nuances explored by this distinguished Argentine researcher, we believe the document in question is valuable; it provides evidence that we have long been visited by these flying objects—objects whose origins we still cannot define.
18TH CENTURY – ANOTHER ACCOUNT
The Paraguayan War was a dramatic and extremely bloody conflict, as all wars are. Argentina, Uruguay, and Brazil participated, resulting in thousands of deaths among the combatants. It was precisely during this era that another significant UFO-related event was recorded in this small country. On November 26, 1866, a Brazilian brig commanded by Captain Augusto Leverger (later honored with the title of Baron of Melgaço) was sailing up the Paraguay River on a wartime mission when, while on deck at night, he observed a phenomenon that defied logical explanation. The event was recorded as follows:
"At 5:47 a.m.," Captain Leverger explains in his report, "with the sky perfectly clear and calm, I spotted a luminous globe that, with incredible speed, traced a 30-degree arc toward the northwest, leaving behind a streak of light in which three distinct bodies could be seen; their brightness was more intense than that of the streak itself and equaled—if it did not exceed—that of a full moon on a clear night. After 25 minutes of observation—during which part of the ship's crew also looked on—everything vanished abruptly, and there were no further atmospheric disturbances thereafter."
"In the city of Asunción," Leverger adds, "I spoke with the Brazilian ambassador and others who corroborated this account." Based on trigonometric calculations applied to the positions personally observed by Leverger, it is estimated that the phenomenon occurred within the atmosphere at a distance of only 59 leagues from Asunción.
This is the notarized text of Captain Leverger's statement. Subsequent inquiries made by the witness with authorities in Asunción determined that the sighting must have taken place in the atmosphere, just 59 leagues distant from the capital, and all investigations determined that the sighting was entirely consistent—and therefore of incalculable value. Through archival research, Marta Virginia Capalló—an Argentine researcher who tracked this event—determined that this might well be the first newspaper report on UFO sightings, predating even a story that appeared in the London *Times* in 1870.
To briefly summarize Captain Leverger’s sighting, it is nearly impossible to believe that the object he observed could have been manufactured using the technology available at the time. We must remember that aircraft only made their debut in the skies during the first decade of the 20th century, and test flights were sporadic. Explanations involving a meteorite or an atmospheric phenomenon also fail to align with Captain Leverger’s account, given the duration of the sighting: a full 25 minutes.
Little is known about the UFO phenomenon within the borders of Paraguay, a small country. Unfortunately, it has often made headlines due to the coup plotters of the day, though—more positively—it is also known for its immense passion for the continent's national sport: soccer.
It is no secret that the UFO phenomenon has a long history; we have frequently cited documents from the era of the Spanish Conquest and accounts by church chroniclers describing sightings and unusual events. These records reinforce the conviction that this phenomenon has always been with us; while its outward form may have changed over time, its essence remains the same—whether one likes it or not.
[Translation ©2026 Insttitute of Hispanic Ufology. Special thanks to Raul Núñez, IIEE]

articles.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
articles.body:
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here.
Introduction
Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.
One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.
The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.
The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.
In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.
The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping.
Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested.
Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction.
Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together.
In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them.
A note about Claude’s methods
In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks.
The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other.
The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model. Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result.
The Hawking-Page transition
To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City.
Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously.
This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave.
To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories. Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics.
This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.
Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from.
Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant, which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature.
At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition.
It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins.
This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information.
In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality.
In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision.) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing?
For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling. This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there.
Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual.
When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops. In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed.
The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result.
To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature.
The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between.
This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all.
Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.)
Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.
Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future.
The modular bootstrap
As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim.
As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10-35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality.
Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one.
Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model, a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems.
In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap, which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.
Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies.
To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension.
The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus.
