articles.title: Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
articles.body:
For years, influencers have come up with workarounds on social media to figure out how to share affiliate links with followers. A new integration between Instagram and Amazon was announced earlier this month as a way to make it easier for influencers to make money from affiliate links — but some content creators are suspicious about who really benefits.
Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
Influencers are now able to link their Amazon and Instagram accounts to promote products. Some are concerned about what they’re opting in to.
The new integration allows creators to connect their Instagram and Amazon accounts and automatically tag products with their affiliate links, from which they earn a commission when followers make purchases. Influencers will be able to embed up to 30 product links in a Reel or 20 in a feed post, but a permissions setting has led to concerns about what creators are actually agreeing to.
In connecting an Amazon account, creators must agree to allow the retailer and its brand sellers to create ads from “any public content” that includes a related affiliate link. Influencers must also agree to acknowledge that brands can edit their content and use their “testimonial, caption or media” for ads.
The wide-ranging permissions are giving creators pause. Some have urged peers not to connect their accounts without reviewing the permissions and understanding how the feature would affect earnings. People making money on social media spend years tweaking their content and strategy to maximize reach, engagement, and, by extension, their bottom line. For some, it appeared that they would be giving Amazon and its sellers the ability to use their content under unclear terms. On Instagram head Adam Mosseri’s post announcing the feature, influencers complained about the lack of clarity, questioned whether using the feature would decrease their reach (which some creators say happens when they link to outside products), and demanded answers to whether their commission rate would stay the same when Amazon or brands use their content for ads.
Linking products through the new integration won’t reduce reach, Jimmy O’Keefe, Instagram’s director of product marketing, said in an email to The Verge. O’Keefe also noted that creators will continue to earn commission through affiliate links when Amazon boosts their posts, and that they can stop the boosting in settings or disconnect the integration entirely. There’s also a separate, manual way to add products without linking accounts, if a creator wants to opt out of having their content made into ads.
Amazon has an enormous influencer program that reaches across social media platforms. It is so lucrative that some content creators are able to make a living almost exclusively by hawking products for sale on Amazon, building empires on the shopping habits of their followers. When it comes to putting those links in front of followers, though, social platforms have historically been a roadblock, hence the cottage industry of link-in-bio tools meant to circumvent limits. Slowly but surely, though, platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube — perhaps chasing the success of TikTok Shop — have added more and more shopping features. The result is that shopping and social media begin to feel more and more like the same thing.

articles.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
articles.body:
Introducing Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed, and verified end-to-end by AI
Abstract
In our previous post, Redwood, we showed that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?”
Today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core.
Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts.
Introduction to interaction nets
Mainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly.
Interaction nets1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because each node has exactly one principal port, no two of these active pairs ever overlap, so they can be rewritten in any order, or all at once, and the result is always the same. Interaction nets are also linear: every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state for the hardware to guard. Languages such as Vine2compile ordinary-looking programs directly to interaction nets. For an excellent introduction to interaction nets and why they suit hardware, we highly recommend Tendrils' “On Interaction Nets.” 3
Fig. 1 shows the difference on a small search problem, placing five queens on a five-by-five board. The sequential program visits one candidate at a time. The interaction net exposes all of its independent work: on average, about twelve interactions are ready to run at every step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get this parallelism; the dependencies were simply never thrown away.
In theory, this should have two large advantages. The first is multithreading for free: rather than varying levels of coarse and fine-grained parallelism, parallelism comes straight from the program. No threads, locks, or race conditions, and none of the out-of-order machinery a conventional core uses to dig it back out. The second is that, since every value has one owner and every step is local, data can live in small local memories next to where it is used. That removes much of the area and power a conventional chip spends on large caching subsystems, and much of the system-level complexity of keeping those caches coherent.
Process
Frostbite was designed with zero architectural priors. We followed the process below, riding multiple agent swarms along the way.
Architecture exploration and selection
To begin architectural exploration, we had to establish the set of workloads Frostbite should do exceedingly well in. We decided to look at different ways a program could expose its work: many independent pieces at once, rounds of parallel work, long sequential chains, data-dependent branches, and recursion. Under each category, we created a search set and a held-out eval set to evaluate the final Frostbite on, ensuring the design generalized to programs it was never tuned on. The kernels for FFT, radixsort, and LU follow the implementation in the SPLASH-2 benchmark, although 64 times smaller, because at regular sizes they are not suitable for exploratory work.
Later, we added five more practical workloads to the held-out set: a Kalman filter, PCA, finite element analysis, an LU solve, and LZ4 decompression.
Agents synthesized research papers and existing benchmarks, and built Python models to trade off high-level architectural ideas against each other, before narrowing to a single architectural concept. The output of this exploration was a 141-page PDF covering the proposed programming model, the runtime, and the high-level blocks of the chip. This was nowhere near the final architecture, but rather a starting point where all the prior findings, high-level requirements, constraints, experiments, and runtime traits were described. Once the first architectural iteration completed (first RTL generation), this was deleted, since many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible.
Formal contracts and system modeling
Once the architecture candidate was selected, our system moved on to building the full software model of the chip. Building software models is essential when exploring an architectural space, as they allow fast iteration between the workloads, the ISA, and the abstracted view of the hardware. Whether we build a CPU, GPU, NPU, or networking switch, mastering this iteration loop allows the fastest exploration of the design space within a finite time. To do this repeatedly, we designed a new in-house specification language, ASL, and wrote Frostbite's system model “Arcmodel” in it. ASL supports machine-checkable translations and refinements between RTL, system models, UVM, SVA, and more, all against a formally backed specification. Its power and performance estimates are accurate to within 1–5%, it runs roughly 200x faster than RTL simulation, and it is formally verifiable through “contracts.”
In every silicon program to date, human architects have written many English PDFs before handing off to an implementation team and a verification team. However, natural language cannot capture every detail an implementation needs precisely and unambiguously, and it cannot guarantee that every agent hallucination is caught while the ASIC is being designed and verified. Natural language was never built for this, and in a world where AI writes the specification, we opt for a formal, machine-checkable specification language instead.
ASL can formally describe both high-level, protocol-like behavior, such as out-of-order handling, CSR programming, memory ordering, and coherency, and low-level details, such as pipelines, arbitration mechanisms, and compute transfer functions. This lets the model leave the specification open-ended where that is useful and constrain it exactly where a precise behavior is required. ASL also translates natively to Lean,4 which we use for all theorem proving when checking AI outputs across RTL, UVM, C, SVA, and more. We will discuss ASL in more detail in a future post.
Throughout the entire development of Frostbite, our AI iterates on the Frostbite ISA, Arcmodel, Design, and Verification tightly together, maintaining the ASL Contract as the source of truth. We've found that having a single, provable source of truth prevents a large class of bugs, silly mistakes, and reward-hacking instances when deploying large agent swarms. Ultimately, this common language allows the models to work across the stack nimbly, reflecting the changes propagated from the workload down to the final hardware. By the end, our Frostbite ASL lowered down to 800k+ lines of Lean.
RTL and alignment
Because ASL is a formally backed specification, designing and verifying the RTL derived from it is the fastest part of the entire Frostbite process. Arcmodel, however, is not physically aware, so its power and performance estimates at first diverge from the true numbers of the timing-converged, synthesis-clean RTL, in the worst case by almost 250%.
Before continuing the ASL autoresearch, one of our systems recalibrates Arcmodel against the RTL. This is a fully autonomous pipeline. It first identifies the power hotspots in the RTL and traces them down to key counters in the formal specification, such as SRAM reads and writes, operation counts, flits sent and received, credit returns, and frame misses. The model may then write any scalar Python function over those counters to predict power, and it repeats this process until the RTL and Arcmodel agree to within 5%.
We find this style of non-gradient learning extremely powerful. Once this first physical alignment has been applied, later iterations are much faster. These are, of course, still pre-silicon power numbers, and over multiple tapeout loops, ASL models can be correlated to true post-silicon, production power numbers.
By aligning the Arcmodel and RTL so closely, the continued swarms were able to explore and exploit much faster. The full Arcmodel chip simulations are much faster than the RTL (660x faster), which led to many cross-stack optimizations. For instance, our AI systems discovered very fine-grained clock gating tricks, and adjusted the software runtime accordingly to accommodate them in a matter of hours. Such a cross-stack optimization is near-impossible to execute on in a traditional ASIC flow.
Contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power, iterated together
Once Arcmodel and the RTL agreed, the original Python models and the architecture PDF were deleted, and the ASL contracts became the only specification of the chip. From then on, contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power moved forward together. Swarms of agents proposed architecture revisions in parallel worktrees; each change was checked against the contracts, modeled in Arcmodel, implemented in RTL, and measured for power, and then either kept or dropped. Across four searches and a final round of ablations, the swarm tried 58 ideas and kept 37 of them, from clock gates on a running tile to smaller L3 tables and one shared expander.
Architectural novelty
The architecture in full detail would warrant its own post. Instead, we choose to focus here on the features that we considered either novel or creative and highlight the capability of our systems to push the frontiers of hardware design.
Programs for Frostbite are written in Vine,2 which is a fully fledged programming language with syntax similar to Rust. A Vine program is compiled to Ivy, an intermediate representation (IR) that encodes the interaction net structure. The optimizer also tries to apply as many of the graph reduction rules as it can, so the final Ivy net, as it is called, has a (mostly) fixed shape, composed of three primitives: data, computation nodes, and control nodes. However, the runtime of this net is still very dynamic, because unlike the typical computation graph, where the parallelism is encoded in the structure and pipelined over time, the parallelism has to be derived at runtime from the state and pipelined spatially. The initial naïve implementations were slow, so our agents had to get creative.
The generated ISA follows from this set of constraints. A lot of it is expected: wide bundles, hardware loop counters, and streams. We found the dynamic features more interesting, particularly operations to take, peek, and copy values from other parts of the net that would be running in parallel. The tiles then come alive, communicating across space.
Emergent property: stealing work
Because the parallelism is spread over space, there is no central scheduler. Instead, we saw the agents design these elegant rules for propagating the work. A tile follows three rules: it runs its own work first, meaning work in its input ports. If those are empty, it takes work from a neighboring tile that has work to spare. If no such tile is found, it can just go inactive and save power.
The agents demonstrated remarkable sophistication in how they implemented this. Below, we have the hardware for a single Frostbite tile:
A lot of them should be familiar. We are interested in the RUNTIME domain that is responsible for the work-stealing behavior described above.
The compiler breaks code into short sections that run uninterrupted once their inputs are ready. These are run in the engine and are mostly organized like traditional computation through the front end. Whenever a loop or branch splits into parallel pieces whose sizes aren't known ahead of time, the running section parks whatever comes after into a small record in local memory, the frame manager. It then drops the new tasks onto a hardware queue called the work queue and picks up the newest one itself. Idle neighbors are then free to pull the remaining tasks over the network. As tasks finish anywhere on the chip in any order, their return packets tick down the parked record's counter and automatically wake the next section the instant the last piece arrives.
This is what it looks like in hardware:
We can think of each “task” as the current board, one level down, with one more queen. Tile 0 has to queue three tasks for all the possible queen configurations before it can finish the present board state. It's free, so it takes the newest task (from itself) and runs it. Meanwhile, its neighbors have gotten the other ones, except for Tile 5, which goes back to sleep.
This behavior was never specified by any human. We can directly trace it back to necessity on specific regressions and hill-climbing performance metrics.
Results
We synthesized Frostbite on a 7 nm process, reaching 800 MHz timing at synthesis and 500 MHz in the final GDS. Each Frostbite quad (a two-by-two grid of tiles) paired with four L3 nodes is 0.792 mm². We benchmark one Quad+L3 cluster against a single core of a modern superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU, which we refer to as TCPU (“Traditional CPU”). This TCPU is 0.895 mm² at the same process.†
We benchmarked on a wide set of workloads, from dense, parallel kernels such as gemm and conv2d, to irregular, branching programs such as JSON parsing, Huffman coding, k-d trees, and recursive Fibonacci. A search set of workloads drove all architectural optimization, ISA design, RTL, and verification, and the chip was evaluated on both the 10 search-set workloads and the 15 held out, including the five practical workloads added later (Fig. 3).
For a fair comparison, we chose to first measure “single-core” performance by benchmarking one Frostbite quad against the TCPU, since they have similar area. Across all the workloads, we average an 8.77x performance-per-area, and across all 25 workloads, search set and held out together, Frostbite reaches a geometric mean of 4.59x the TCPU's performance-per-watt: 6.02x on the 10 search-set workloads, and 3.83x on the 15 held-out workloads it was never tuned on. As expected, the architecture does most strongly on highly parallelizable tasks, but it also outperforms the TCPU on branching, dynamic code.
The energy breakdown shows where the savings come from. Leaving out clock distribution (49% of TCPU energy, 41% of a Frostbite quad's), the TCPU spends 57% of its energy on memory and 27% on fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions. Frostbite cuts memory to 38% and fetch, decode, and issue to just 6%. In exchange, it spends 26% on its on-chip network and scheduler, the cost of sharing work and moving messages between tiles. What's more exciting, however, is that as we scale the chip to a four-by-four array (four quads), the power distribution is relatively the same. In a general-purpose multi-core CPU arrangement, scaling the number of cores requires adding heavy coherency mechanisms and large caches, whereas when running interaction nets, the same data locality rules always apply, and more cores do not increase system complexity. This is illustrated below. In the coming months, we'll be benchmarking Frostbite mesh-like configurations against multi-core “TCPU” arrangements with large caches and larger, wider, out-of-order CPUs, over a larger set of industry benchmarks such as SPEC and PARSEC.
What comes next
While interaction nets have been around for more than 35 years, their production value has never been fully clear. Historically, there has always been a risk of exploring out-of-distribution architectures, for the time, investment, and labor required to come to conviction. We believe AI fundamentally changes these economics. In the search for higher performance and lower power, extreme co-design of workloads, ISA, and hardware will continue to be demanded. With large agent swarms, sophisticated search-space techniques, precise guardrails, formal verification, and faster EDA tools, AI systems will be able to discover and build novel accelerators at a quality that exceeds human cognition. While there is much more to do, we feel it is the right time to share with the world what the future of autonomous chip design could look like. We plan to continue scaling development on Frostbite, including but not limited to:
- Deliver a software playground for anybody to run a program on Frostbite, hosted on FPGAs.
- Build a preliminary operating system capable of managing hardware resources, multiple programs, virtualization, and more.
- Scale swarms to bring Frostbite to higher performance-per-watt, and benchmark it on a much larger set of workloads against a broader set of CPUs.
- Release the RTL and ISA for Frostbite.
We are having a lot of fun!
Notes
†For legal reasons, we cannot disclose the exact CPU.
References
- 1.Lafont, Y. (1990). “Interaction Nets.” Proceedings of the 17th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL ’90), 95–108. doi:10.1145/96709.96718
- 2.The Vine programming language. vine.dev
- 3.Tendrils (2026). “On Interaction Nets.” tendrils.co/blog/2026-04-26/on-inets
- 4.de Moura, L., and Ullrich, S. (2021). “The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language.” Automated Deduction – CADE 28, LNCS 12699, 625–635. doi:10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37
Partner with us
If your edge depends on the silicon underneath it, whether you're an AI lab, a fabless chip company, an OEM, a defense prime, or ASIC design partner, we want to hear from you.

The kernels for FFT, radixsort, and LU follow the implementation in the SPLASH-2 benchmark, although 64 times smaller, because at regular sizes they are not suitable for exploratory work.
Later, we added five more practical workloads to the held-out set: a Kalman filter, PCA, finite element analysis, an LU solve, and LZ4 decompression.
Agents synthesized research papers and existing benchmarks, and built Python models to trade off high-level architectural ideas against each other, before narrowing to a single architectural concept. The output of this exploration was a 141-page PDF covering the proposed programming model, the runtime, and the high-level blocks of the chip. This was nowhere near the final architecture, but rather a starting point where all the prior findings, high-level requirements, constraints, experiments, and runtime traits were described. Once the first architectural iteration completed (first RTL generation), this was deleted, since many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible.
Formal contracts and system modeling
Once the architecture candidate was selected, our system moved on to building the full software model of the chip. Building software models is essential when exploring an architectural space, as they allow fast iteration between the workloads, the ISA, and the abstracted view of the hardware. Whether we build a CPU, GPU, NPU, or networking switch, mastering this iteration loop allows the fastest exploration of the design space within a finite time. To do this repeatedly, we designed a new in-house specification language, ASL, and wrote Frostbite's system model “Arcmodel” in it. ASL supports machine-checkable translations and refinements between RTL, system models, UVM, SVA, and more, all against a formally backed specification. Its power and performance estimates are accurate to within 1–5%, it runs roughly 200x faster than RTL simulation, and it is formally verifiable through “contracts.”
In every silicon program to date, human architects have written many English PDFs before handing off to an implementation team and a verification team. However, natural language cannot capture every detail an implementation needs precisely and unambiguously, and it cannot guarantee that every agent hallucination is caught while the ASIC is being designed and verified. Natural language was never built for this, and in a world where AI writes the specification, we opt for a formal, machine-checkable specification language instead.
ASL can formally describe both high-level, protocol-like behavior, such as out-of-order handling, CSR programming, memory ordering, and coherency, and low-level details, such as pipelines, arbitration mechanisms, and compute transfer functions. This lets the model leave the specification open-ended where that is useful and constrain it exactly where a precise behavior is required. ASL also translates natively to Lean,4 which we use for all theorem proving when checking AI outputs across RTL, UVM, C, SVA, and more. We will discuss ASL in more detail in a future post.
Throughout the entire development of Frostbite, our AI iterates on the Frostbite ISA, Arcmodel, Design, and Verification tightly together, maintaining the ASL Contract as the source of truth. We've found that having a single, provable source of truth prevents a large class of bugs, silly mistakes, and reward-hacking instances when deploying large agent swarms. Ultimately, this common language allows the models to work across the stack nimbly, reflecting the changes propagated from the workload down to the final hardware. By the end, our Frostbite ASL lowered down to 800k+ lines of Lean.
RTL and alignment
Because ASL is a formally backed specification, designing and verifying the RTL derived from it is the fastest part of the entire Frostbite process. Arcmodel, however, is not physically aware, so its power and performance estimates at first diverge from the true numbers of the timing-converged, synthesis-clean RTL, in the worst case by almost 250%.
Before continuing the ASL autoresearch, one of our systems recalibrates Arcmodel against the RTL. This is a fully autonomous pipeline. It first identifies the power hotspots in the RTL and traces them down to key counters in the formal specification, such as SRAM reads and writes, operation counts, flits sent and received, credit returns, and frame misses. The model may then write any scalar Python function over those counters to predict power, and it repeats this process until the RTL and Arcmodel agree to within 5%.
We find this style of non-gradient learning extremely powerful. Once this first physical alignment has been applied, later iterations are much faster. These are, of course, still pre-silicon power numbers, and over multiple tapeout loops, ASL models can be correlated to true post-silicon, production power numbers.
By aligning the Arcmodel and RTL so closely, the continued swarms were able to explore and exploit much faster. The full Arcmodel chip simulations are much faster than the RTL (660x faster), which led to many cross-stack optimizations. For instance, our AI systems discovered very fine-grained clock gating tricks, and adjusted the software runtime accordingly to accommodate them in a matter of hours. Such a cross-stack optimization is near-impossible to execute on in a traditional ASIC flow.
Contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power, iterated together
Once Arcmodel and the RTL agreed, the original Python models and the architecture PDF were deleted, and the ASL contracts became the only specification of the chip. From then on, contracts, Arcmodel, RTL, and power moved forward together. Swarms of agents proposed architecture revisions in parallel worktrees; each change was checked against the contracts, modeled in Arcmodel, implemented in RTL, and measured for power, and then either kept or dropped. Across four searches and a final round of ablations, the swarm tried 58 ideas and kept 37 of them, from clock gates on a running tile to smaller L3 tables and one shared expander.
Architectural novelty
The architecture in full detail would warrant its own post. Instead, we choose to focus here on the features that we considered either novel or creative and highlight the capability of our systems to push the frontiers of hardware design.
Programs for Frostbite are written in Vine,2 which is a fully fledged programming language with syntax similar to Rust. A Vine program is compiled to Ivy, an intermediate representation (IR) that encodes the interaction net structure. The optimizer also tries to apply as many of the graph reduction rules as it can, so the final Ivy net, as it is called, has a (mostly) fixed shape, composed of three primitives: data, computation nodes, and control nodes. However, the runtime of this net is still very dynamic, because unlike the typical computation graph, where the parallelism is encoded in the structure and pipelined over time, the parallelism has to be derived at runtime from the state and pipelined spatially. The initial naïve implementations were slow, so our agents had to get creative.
The generated ISA follows from this set of constraints. A lot of it is expected: wide bundles, hardware loop counters, and streams. We found the dynamic features more interesting, particularly operations to take, peek, and copy values from other parts of the net that would be running in parallel. The tiles then come alive, communicating across space.
Emergent property: stealing work
Because the parallelism is spread over space, there is no central scheduler. Instead, we saw the agents design these elegant rules for propagating the work. A tile follows three rules: it runs its own work first, meaning work in its input ports. If those are empty, it takes work from a neighboring tile that has work to spare. If no such tile is found, it can just go inactive and save power.
The agents demonstrated remarkable sophistication in how they implemented this. Below, we have the hardware for a single Frostbite tile:
A lot of them should be familiar. We are interested in the RUNTIME domain that is responsible for the work-stealing behavior described above.
The compiler breaks code into short sections that run uninterrupted once their inputs are ready. These are run in the engine and are mostly organized like traditional computation through the front end. Whenever a loop or branch splits into parallel pieces whose sizes aren't known ahead of time, the running section parks whatever comes after into a small record in local memory, the frame manager. It then drops the new tasks onto a hardware queue called the work queue and picks up the newest one itself. Idle neighbors are then free to pull the remaining tasks over the network. As tasks finish anywhere on the chip in any order, their return packets tick down the parked record's counter and automatically wake the next section the instant the last piece arrives.
This is what it looks like in hardware:
We can think of each “task” as the current board, one level down, with one more queen. Tile 0 has to queue three tasks for all the possible queen configurations before it can finish the present board state. It's free, so it takes the newest task (from itself) and runs it. Meanwhile, its neighbors have gotten the other ones, except for Tile 5, which goes back to sleep.
This behavior was never specified by any human. We can directly trace it back to necessity on specific regressions and hill-climbing performance metrics.
Results
We synthesized Frostbite on a 7 nm process, reaching 800 MHz timing at synthesis and 500 MHz in the final GDS. Each Frostbite quad (a two-by-two grid of tiles) paired with four L3 nodes is 0.792 mm². We benchmark one Quad+L3 cluster against a single core of a modern superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU, which we refer to as TCPU (“Traditional CPU”). This TCPU is 0.895 mm² at the same process.†
We benchmarked on a wide set of workloads, from dense, parallel kernels such as gemm and conv2d, to irregular, branching programs such as JSON parsing, Huffman coding, k-d trees, and recursive Fibonacci. A search set of workloads drove all architectural optimization, ISA design, RTL, and verification, and the chip was evaluated on both the 10 search-set workloads and the 15 held out, including the five practical workloads added later (Fig. 3).
For a fair comparison, we chose to first measure “single-core” performance by benchmarking one Frostbite quad against the TCPU, since they have similar area. Across all the workloads, we average an 8.77x performance-per-area, and across all 25 workloads, search set and held out together, Frostbite reaches a geometric mean of 4.59x the TCPU's performance-per-watt: 6.02x on the 10 search-set workloads, and 3.83x on the 15 held-out workloads it was never tuned on. As expected, the architecture does most strongly on highly parallelizable tasks, but it also outperforms the TCPU on branching, dynamic code.
The energy breakdown shows where the savings come from. Leaving out clock distribution (49% of TCPU energy, 41% of a Frostbite quad's), the TCPU spends 57% of its energy on memory and 27% on fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions. Frostbite cuts memory to 38% and fetch, decode, and issue to just 6%. In exchange, it spends 26% on its on-chip network and scheduler, the cost of sharing work and moving messages between tiles. What's more exciting, however, is that as we scale the chip to a four-by-four array (four quads), the power distribution is relatively the same. In a general-purpose multi-core CPU arrangement, scaling the number of cores requires adding heavy coherency mechanisms and large caches, whereas when running interaction nets, the same data locality rules always apply, and more cores do not increase system complexity. This is illustrated below. In the coming months, we'll be benchmarking Frostbite mesh-like configurations against multi-core “TCPU” arrangements with large caches and larger, wider, out-of-order CPUs, over a larger set of industry benchmarks such as SPEC and PARSEC.
What comes next
While interaction nets have been around for more than 35 years, their production value has never been fully clear. Historically, there has always been a risk of exploring out-of-distribution architectures, for the time, investment, and labor required to come to conviction. We believe AI fundamentally changes these economics. In the search for higher performance and lower power, extreme co-design of workloads, ISA, and hardware will continue to be demanded. With large agent swarms, sophisticated search-space techniques, precise guardrails, formal verification, and faster EDA tools, AI systems will be able to discover and build novel accelerators at a quality that exceeds human cognition. While there is much more to do, we feel it is the right time to share with the world what the future of autonomous chip design could look like. We plan to continue scaling development on Frostbite, including but not limited to:
- Deliver a software playground for anybody to run a program on Frostbite, hosted on FPGAs.
- Build a preliminary operating system capable of managing hardware resources, multiple programs, virtualization, and more.
- Scale swarms to bring Frostbite to higher performance-per-watt, and benchmark it on a much larger set of workloads against a broader set of CPUs.
- Release the RTL and ISA for Frostbite.
We are having a lot of fun!
Notes
†For legal reasons, we cannot disclose the exact CPU.
References
- 1.Lafont, Y. (1990). “Interaction Nets.” Proceedings of the 17th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL ’90), 95–108. doi:10.1145/96709.96718
- 2.The Vine programming language. vine.dev
- 3.Tendrils (2026). “On Interaction Nets.” tendrils.co/blog/2026-04-26/on-inets
- 4.de Moura, L., and Ullrich, S. (2021). “The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language.” Automated Deduction – CADE 28, LNCS 12699, 625–635. doi:10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37
Partner with us
If your edge depends on the silicon underneath it, whether you're an AI lab, a fabless chip company, an OEM, a defense prime, or ASIC design partner, we want to hear from you.

articles.title: Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented
articles.body:
EXTRA, extra! Today I’m launching Future Stories, my own podcast about technology, science and the way we live.
The first guest is Vint Cerf. He co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn in the 1970s, the rules that let the world’s networks talk to each other. Interviewing him was on my bucket list for years. When I was at Cloudflare I thought about asking him many times, but I was a bit shy. He’s Vint Cerf, after all. This year I finally asked, and he said yes.
We talked over Zoom (not using Zoom again) on October 14. He’s 83, he left Google this year after more than twenty years, and he’s helping start a company, Tolero, that is building software for an Internet between planets. His words: “the speed of light is too slow.”
“Who will our allies be 25 years from now? And we didn’t know. So we thought the only way we can be assured that the allies will have access to this is to simply open it up.”
Some peculiar stories from the conversation
First, a bug related one (ring a bell? those never stopped over the years…). Vint once spent two weeks on a program that failed at random, so he couldn’t reproduce it. He finally asked his best friend, Steve Crocker, to step through it with him. At one point Crocker said “that’s the problem”, and he was right. Thirty seconds, after two weeks. Vint’s takeaway is that this is why collaboration matters.
Then a bottle of glitter. In late 1989 three commercial Internet services started in the United States, and one of them was called CERFnet, in San Diego. They first wanted to call it SURFnet, because surfing the Internet, but a network in the Netherlands had a name too close to it. So they asked Vint if they could use his.
He had a moment of “what if they screw it up?”, then decided that people name kids after other people and nobody blames the person they were named after. At the launch, he and the network’s director smashed a plastic bottle of glitter over a Cisco router.
He also tried to connect Minitel, the French online service, to MCI Mail, the email service he built in the 1980s. MCI Mail was designed to link to everything. It reached the telegraph system, which he calls 19th-century stuff, and fax. It even reached the post office: type a postal address into the email and they printed it, put it in an envelope and mailed it. Minitel refused to connect, and he says he still doesn’t understand why.
One more, from outside the interview: In 2020, someone on the Internet-history mailing list (I’m on it) asked if anyone had ever seen Vint without a three-piece suit. One reply: “I have seen Vint in a t-shirt!” Vint answered with just a photo, “IP on Everything”, from a 1992 engineers’ meeting where, in his words, he “felt compelled” to do an “IP on Everything” striptease. The thread is public.
We didn’t go very deep into AI. Time was short, and it’s not his main field these days. But even there, he has a clear way of thinking about it. And near the end he shows a piece of the original ARPANET on camera, and talks about his worry that the next century won’t be able to read what we leave behind.
“I’m worried that the 22nd century won’t know what happened in the 21st because all of our records will have evaporated or will be uninterpretable.”
The full conversation is 56 minutes, with chapters:
You can also read the transcript at ourfuturestories.eu/vint-cerf, or listen in your favourite podcast app: ourfuturestories.eu/subscribe. A Portuguese article about it is on SAPO. Short clips are coming in the next days.
This is a passion project. The idea is to tell good stories, the kind that hold up over time. If you like it, subscribe, share it with a friend, and tell me who I should talk to next, you can do it here: ourfuturestories.eu/#contact.
Stay tuned, geek out!
———
Fun fact: in 2024 I did a segment on the 50 years of the TCP paper on my previous podcast, This Week in NET at Cloudflare. My guests were three then-colleagues: Mark Nottingham (standards), Marwan Fayed (research) and Lucas Pardue (web protocols, co-chair of the IETF’s QUIC working group). You can listen here (or below).
The paper is “A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication”, by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, published in May 1974 in IEEE Transactions on Communications. It described TCP, a way to join many packet networks into a network of networks. TCP was later split into TCP and IP, and in 1983 they became the core of the Internet that DARPA launched.

articles.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
articles.body:
A virus has stopped pancreatic cancer in its tracks in three people in a clinical trial in the US. Further evaluation is needed in larger trials, but the early results are encouraging, especially since only small doses of the virus were administered for initial safety testing.
“We only injected one-tenth of the dose we are eventually aiming at, so the efficacy is better than I expected, especially as this is pancreatic cancer,” says Masato Yamamoto at the University of Minnesota, who led the development of the viral treatment.
Pancreatic cancer is notorious for being the deadliest type of the condition. One reason is that symptoms tend to appear late, when the cancer has already spread and cannot be surgically removed. Once diagnosed, people usually live only around three to six months.
Advertisement
Another reason is that pancreatic tumours have tough, fibrous exteriors that block chemotherapy drugs from getting in. “They’re hard as hockey pucks,” says Yamamoto. Immunotherapies that boost immune activity against cancer are also ineffective, because pancreatic tumours can hide from the immune system.
The first patient in the trial, who had a pancreatic tumour 7 centimetres across, was administered the treatment a year ago, and the other two have been since then. At the time, their tumours hadn’t spread beyond the pancreas. Since being treated, their tumours haven’t grown any further. “They are all still alive and have clinically stable disease,” says Yamamoto, who presented the results at the annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy in Boston, Massachusetts, earlier this month. Another 15 patients will now be given higher doses to find the optimum level.
“I think this is an interesting early signal, but as a pancreatic surgeon, I think it’s important to keep perspective,” says Kai Brown at Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney. “The history of oncology is littered with promising early signals that vanished by the time rigorous phase III [late-stage] testing was done, so I think these preliminary conference results should probably just be seen as hypothesis-generating at this stage.” He also notes that the trial so far hasn’t included a control group, so it is hard to know whether the cancer-killing virus works better than other treatments or none at all.
The virus is an adenovirus that has been genetically engineered to replicate only inside tumours and not healthy tissue. Its replication is specifically activated by an enzyme called cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which is present at much higher levels in cancer cells than in normal ones. After cancer cells become infected with the virus, they burst open and die, releasing more virus that can infect neighbouring cancer cells.
In the trial, the virus was injected directly into the patients’ tumours through a thin tube that was guided down a patient’s throat to their pancreas. The tube had an ultrasound probe on the end to allow visualisation of the tumours.
The reason the tumours have stopped growing but haven’t become any smaller may be due to the low treatment dose, says Yamamoto. He thinks they may start to shrink as the virus has more time to replicate.
As the tumour cells start to break apart and leak their contents, the immune system may also be able to recognise and fight the cancer, says Yamamoto. “The patient’s immune system can realise something is wrong, and then go and attack the tumour,” he says. The hope is that the immune system will also recognise and destroy any tumour cells that have spread to other parts of the body. If so, the treatment could be effective against metastatic pancreatic cancer.
To try to supercharge this natural immune response, Yamamoto and his colleagues are now planning to combine the viral treatment with immunotherapies like checkpoint inhibitors – drugs that block proteins that stop the immune system from attacking the cancer cells – in future clinical trials.
Adenoviruses, which cause cold- and flu-like symptoms in their unmodified forms, have a long history of being investigated as potential cancer treatments. In the 1950s, for instance, women with cervical cancer were injected with an unmodified adenovirus in a clinical trial, with partial success. However, it became clear that adenoviruses must be engineered to make them selectively target cancer cells, for safety and efficacy reasons.
The only cancer-killing virus that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in the US is T-VEC, a genetically modified herpes simplex virus that is injected directly into melanoma tumours, causing the cells to rupture and die.

articles.title: UN court cites military Facebook posts while finding Myanmar guilty of genocide
articles.body:
In its ruling that Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya people in 2016 and 2017, the United Nations’ top court says that Facebook played a role in helping Myanmar’s military spread hate speech against its Muslim minority. The ruling from the International Court of Justice determined that Facebook posts made by the country’s military “dehumanized” the Muslim minority “and at times encouraged and legitimized violence against them,” as reported earlier by Reuters.
UN court cites military Facebook posts while finding Myanmar guilty of genocide
Posts across Facebook ‘dehumanized’ the Rohingya Muslim people, the UN’s top court has found.
The decision that Myanmar committed genocide comes after The Gambia sued the country in 2019 over the military’s violent “clearance operations” targeting the Rohingya Muslims. The military relied heavily on Facebook, which was the most popular platform in Myanmar at the time of the attacks, with a 2022 report from Amnesty International finding that the platform “proactively amplified and promoted content on the Facebook platform which incited violence, hatred, and discrimination against the Rohingya.” Despite numerous warnings from human rights activists, Amnesty International said Facebook failed to stop the spread of hateful content in Myanmar.
The UN is now backing up these findings. It cites a report from the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), which says that a post made by the military ahead of its August 25th, 2017 massacres on the Rohingya people “unleashed a torrent of public vitriol,” with over 200 comments calling for Rohingya people “to be shot, killed, exterminated or permanently removed from Myanmar.”
Facebook later removed military-linked pages containing thousands of posts with anti-Rohingya hate speech published between July and December 2017, according to the IIMM. The company admitted in 2018 that it didn’t do enough to prevent the incitement of violence in Myanmar, and later introduced a “corporate human rights policy” that includes an annual report about its impact on human rights. The Verge reached out to Meta with a request for comment but didn’t immediately hear back.

articles.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
articles.body:
California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of the company’s former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.
The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added.
The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).
The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.
The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government itself is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.
The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.
Democrat representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

articles.title: The Big Idea: Melissa Poett
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Melissa Poett
Posted on November 19, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 1 Comment
What’s better than a whip-smart, whip-wielding protagonist? One who uses those skills to combat injustice and help those in need. Robin Hood fans rejoice, for author Melissa Poett has brought us a dystopian, femme-fatale retelling, without the merry men. Clutch your coin purses and follow along in the Big Idea for A Thief to Die For.
MELISSA POETT:
When you hear the name Robin Hood, perhaps you think about a revolution. Or maybe it’s more specific—you think of a medieval man who was radicalized to defend the powerless against the tyranny of the corrupt elite. A hero. A leader. Maybe even a criminal, an outlaw who was willing to break the rules to right the scales of justice in a tale as old as time, and one that, unfortunately, remains timely.
I, too, think of all those things. And yet, I was also left with a question: how would that story have unfolded differently if the same revolution was led by a woman?
More specifically, Marian.
A Thief to Die For is my reimagining of Robin Hood set in a dystopian world. It’s about a whip-wielding Marian who has made it her mission to sabotage her tyrant father, while risking the kind of love wars are fought over.
True to the original legend of Robin Hood, injustice is the catalyst. Except, it wasn’t killing a deer in the King’s forest or a fight with the sheriff’s men that started this rebellion. In A Thief to Die For, Marian is radicalized by growing up under her horrific father—a tyrant who runs a slave operation in a coal mine. And her simmering rage is why she steals from his wagons to help the people trapped under his control.
But this is where the story you know and love takes an unconventional turn. Where Robin Hood showcases his mastery of the bow and arrow while recruiting an army of charismatic men to fight with him, Marian’s path as the heroine looks quite different. I imagine she would move through the world sacrificially—like a woman.
This isn’t a spoiler, so don’t worry. But it is the foundation to Marian’s character. In a world where she can’t dethrone her father without bringing the house of cards down, she must think outside the box. Move strategically. Outsmart the powerful, while prioritizing the weakest around her. She’s an everyday woman considering all the consequences of a confrontation, and every way it could go wrong. Is she capable of violence? Yes, occasionally. Especially when she secretly raids. Is she excellent with her weapon of choice—a whip? Most definitely. But as any number of women can tell you, there’s a moral burden we carry that isn’t seen in the original folktale of Robin Hood. It means Marian’s revolt is exercised in the shadows as she prioritizes the protection of the people around her. There is no ever-growing army of people joining her rebellion. Marian sacrifices herself by raiding alone.
Which brings me to the next significant shift in the narrative, an epic love story. Yes, I can hear you reminding me that the original folktale did include romance. You’re right; Robin Hood got the girl in the end. But I’m not talking about some proverbial cherry on top of an already half-eaten sundae. I’m talking about an epic love so foundational to the story that it’s as consequential as taking down the villain. Give me yearning. Break my heart.
Now that’s the kind of reimagining I want to read—a story of Robin Hood, a revolution reimagined. But this time through the lens of Marian’s sacrifice and epic love.
—-
A Thief to Die For: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Powell’s|Canada Pre-order|UK Pre-order

articles.title: I'll never buy Framework hardware again
articles.body:
TL;DR:
We bought a 3000 EUR Framework Laptop 16 for one of our developers. It was broken out of the box. Three months, around thirty support emails, two replacement parts and a trip to their repair center later, Framework concluded “No Fault Found” and blamed the keyboard layout of an OS that wasn’t even installed when the problem first showed up. I’m done with them.
Some context first#
I have been a Framework fan for a while. At my company, several of our developers work on Framework laptops or desktops, we have about quite a few of them around, and I have been recommending them to pretty much anyone who asked me what laptop to buy so far. Repairable hardware, Linux-friendly, a company that seemed to care about the people using its products: it was an easy recommendation to make.
So when Q joined the team and needed a workstation, we ordered a Framework Laptop 16, around 3000 EUR once configured.
Three months later, I’m pissed off at Framework and have banned future purchases from them at my company. Not because the machine arrived broken, this happens and I’ve been around hardware long enough to know it, but because of how unprofessional and useless the support has been from the first email to the last.
OH and feel free to share, friends don’t let friends enter hell.
Day one: broken out of the box#
The laptop arrives early August. Q assembles it, powers it on and is greeted by a “missing input module” screen, before reaching the BIOS, before any operating system is even installed. Keep this detail in mind, we’ll get back to it.
The keyboard isn’t detected when centered, and when moved to the left it shows up as… a numpad. In that state, nothing works: not the keyboard, not the touchpad, not the numpad. There’s a BIOS option, “Force Power for Input Modules”, that bypasses module detection. With it enabled, everything works. Without it, the machine has no keyboard and no touchpad. It is recommended NOT to turn it on permanently as it might be harmful to the hardware, as stated on their own website.
I open a ticket on August 13th.
August: the script loop hell#
What follows is two weeks of support reading from a script, one step per email, one email per day or two:
- is it out of the box? any damage on the packaging? which OS, which kernel, which BIOS version?
- do a mainboard reset by pressing the chassis switch ten times
- reseat the midplate
- try Force Power On (we had already told them it was the only thing that worked)
- send photos of the keyboard, the midplate, the connector, the whole laptop from six angles, and a video
- reset the BIOS to defaults
- reinstall the BIOS and the drivers bundle (a Windows drivers bundle, for a problem that happens before any OS boots, on a machine that doesn’t run Windows…)
- try different input module combinations
We did all of it. We sent the photos and the video in a shared drive. Each reply came from a different agent who clearly hadn’t read the thread, and asked for something we had already provided.
On August 24th I lost patience and wrote that this was a 3000 EUR laptop that didn’t work, that my co-worker had been without a usable machine for over a week, and asked them to either send replacement parts or take it back and refund us. I even went all Karen and asked to involve a manager.
Their answer: please send a clear photo of the midplate and the underside of the keyboard. The same photos, again. No manager involved to break the script because no flying fucks were given.
We did their diagnosis for them#
Q then replied from his own address, which apparently is a problem, because support spent the next ten days asking him to “verify the shipping address” of the order, which he did, several times.
Meanwhile, tired of being asked to repeat steps,
he updated the keyboard firmware himself (only possible with Force Power On, since the keyboard is otherwise not detected),
installed Framework’s own framework_tool,
and ran a proper isolation:
$ sudo framework_tool --inputdeck
The result was unambiguous:
the keyboard module reports the ID of a numpad, KeyboardB.
The firmware therefore sees two numpads and no keyboard,
considers the input deck incomplete,
and never enables the power rail for the input modules,
which is why everything is dead and not just the keyboard.
He moved the keyboard alone across slots: it misidentifies itself in every position. He moved the numpad alone into the same slot: it identifies correctly. He removed everything: the baseline is clean. The wrong ID follows the keyboard. The keyboard is faulty.
He sent all of this to support on August 28th with a full report and a one-line reproduction command.
September: they replace the wrong part#
On September 7th, support concludes… that the midplate needs to be replaced. Not the keyboard, the only part that a reproducible diagnostic, run with their own tool, had just pointed at.
The midplate arrives a week later. The problem is, of course, still there because… GOTO previous paragraph. Q asks them whether they’re sure it’s not the keyboard, given that he proved it with the diagnosis.
Their answer ?
Back to the queue. Back to photos: the packaging box from different angles including the interior, the midplate front and back, the keyboard top and bottom, close-ups of the sockets. Photos they already had.
At this point, Q is no longer a developer but has become a profesionnal photographer.
October: a new keyboard, a new bug#
On October 8th, two months after the laptop arrived, Framework finally agrees to replace the keyboard. What they should have done on the first week…
The new keyboard is detected, the original bug is gone,
but there is a new one:
pressing C sends a c followed by a Delete escape sequence.
$ showkey -a
c       99 0143 0x63
^[[3~   27 0033 0x1b
        91 0133 0x5b
        51 0063 0x33
       126 0176 0x7e
An external keyboard on the same machine produces a single c, as it should.
FU-CKIN’ HELL it never ends…
You can’t use a keyboard where typing a word containing a c deletes the next character.
You certainly can’t type a disk encryption passphrase with it.
Q is smart so he knows the drill and sends the showkey output, photos, and a video to avoid wasting time on a useless round-trip,
but he understimated them:
support asks him whether the issue happens with an external keyboard (he had already said it didn’t),
then asks him to boot a live USB to “isolate software issues” (yes, the famous ones that would trigger on just their keyboard).
He does, tries both the US and French layouts, same result as anyone not brain-dead would expect.
The ticket is escalated, with the usual “escalations may take 5 to 7 working days”.
November: “No Fault Found”#
End of October, Framework decides to have the laptop sent to their repair center for a “full review and assessment”, with a reminder that we may be charged if they find customer-induced damage.
We ship it.
This morning, November 20th, the verdict arrives:
Our repair center has completed their diagnostics, tested two keyboards and found that they were working perfectly. They have determined No Fault Found and that the issue was likely caused by installing the wrong keyboard layout in the operating system.
Let me be very clear about why this is nonsense:
- Keyboard 1 failed before any operating system was installed on the machine. The “missing input module” screen shows up before the BIOS. There was no keyboard layout to get wrong. However, the BIOS workaround they asked us to enable was still on when the laptop was shipped, and with it on, the problem is hidden. If you don’t turn it off, you won’t see the fault.
- Keyboard 2 fails in GRUB, before the kernel is even loaded, and on a live USB with both QWERTY and AZERTY layouts, which, by the way, put the C key in the same place. A keyboard layout maps a key to a character; it does not make a key emit two scancodes. And if you test by typing a sentence and looking at the result, a spurious Delete at the end of a line deletes nothing and you’ll never notice it. You have to actually look at what the key sends, which is exactly what we showed them.
So either the repair center tested with the workaround on and never pressed C in the middle of a word, or they didn’t test at all. In both cases, “the user picked the wrong keyboard layout” is not a diagnosis, it’s a way to close a ticket.
What it cost us#
Let’s count:
- three months and one week since the laptop arrived,
- around thirty emails from support, handled by more than a dozen different agents,
- two replacement parts, one of which was the wrong one,
- a round trip to a repair center,
- hours of an engineer’s time spent producing photos, videos, reports and diagnostics that the support team then didn’t read,
- a developer who had to work for weeks with external devices plugged into a laptop that couldn’t be used as a laptop.
And at the end, the laptop comes back in the exact state it left, with a note implying we don’t know how to configure a keyboard layout.
The problem isn’t the hardware#
Hardware fails. A bad keyboard module out of the box is annoying, not scandalous. I’ve had DOA hardware from every vendor I’ve ever bought from.
What’s scandalous is the process:
- nobody owns the ticket, every reply comes from someone new who restarts from a script;
- information we provide is not read, so it gets requested again, and again;
- a clear, reproducible diagnosis made with their own tool is ignored in favor of replacing an unrelated part;
- basic customer identity handling is broken enough that a colleague replying on the thread triggers ten days of address verification;
- and when it finally reaches people who could actually look at the hardware, the conclusion contradicts facts that were in the ticket from day one.
What’s scandalous is the amount of not giving a damn, not escalating, not caring at all about having a customer in a shit situation for more than three months when they could simply replace the broken part and be done. Like they can’t afford a spare keyboard and make sure that it works ?
So, what now?#
We’re not going to spend another three months trying to get Framework to acknowledge a fault we’ve demonstrated a dozen times when they obviously don’t care. We’ll recycle the laptop into a desktop when it comes back from the repair center and will get Q a new laptop from another vendor that’s more serious and professional.
As for me: buying new Framework hardware is now off the table. The machines we have will live their lives, but the next ones will come from somewhere else.
I liked the idea of Framework a lot. Repairability is worthless if the company behind it can’t tell a broken keyboard from a keyboard layout nor… repair, and the support I’ve experienced is the opposite of what I’d expect from a company selling premium-priced hardware to professionals.
If you’re considering a Framework for your company, I hope it works out of the box for you. Because if it doesn’t, you now know what’s waiting for you.

articles.title: Llms.txt and MCP didn't move the needle
articles.body:
Two years ago, an admin panel for a simple website took me a day, maybe two - and I was proud of how fast I was. Now it takes me about...
Two years ago, an admin panel for a simple website took me a day, maybe two - and I was proud of how fast I was. Now it takes me about an hour or two.
The old day went like this. Install the package, generate the CRUDs, configure every field and column, wire up the relationships, click through everything to check it works. Thirty to sixty minutes per CRUD, easily. Now I describe what I want, the agent runs our generators, writes the configuration, writes the tests, and I review. A day of work fits in an hour. A week-long feature fits in a day.
I'm not the only one seeing this. In February 2026, a customer from New Zealand gave us a 10 out of 10 in our feedback form. The whole review was one line:
"Straightforward to use (particularly with Claude looking over my shoulder!)"
That's the new normal. The developer isn't alone with the docs anymore. There's an agent next to them that already knows the package.
I maintain Backpack for Laravel, an admin panel package that's been around for 10 years. We did a bunch of things to make the AI agents better at writing admin panels with Backpack - it's a quick-moving niche. But when I looked at why AI agents are so good at it, the answer surprised me. Most of it isn't the AI-specific stuff we built. Two of the things everyone tells you to add, llms.txt and an MCP server, barely helped us at all.
Here's what did help, so you can do the same for your package.
Let's get these out of the way first, because most "make your package AI-ready" advice starts with them.
llms.txt. We shipped one. I don't think it does much. Agents rarely go looking for it. When they do, they find a table of contents for docs they could already read. Thinking of removing it, tbh.
An MCP server. We built one so agents could query our docs. The results were mixed at best. The agent has to decide to call it, and it usually doesn't. Then the queries some of the AIs make are... laughable. Of course our MCP doesn't return anything useful, your AI just typed two words - absurd! So no, I don't think our MCP is helpul any more - thinking of removing it too, tbh. An MCP server is a great fit for live data the agent can't get any other way - or tool use. Static documentation isn't that.
The lesson: anything the agent has to remember to go fetch is weak. What works is what's already in front of it, or already in its head.
Our biggest wins came from decisions we made years before anyone used AI to write code.
Backpack's core API has barely changed in the last four years. Even v8, which we're working on right now, started with maintenance: bumping and removing dependencies, fixing inconsistencies. The way you define a field or a column stays the same. We did that to make upgrades painless for old projects. The side effect: years of Backpack code ended up in model training data, and all of it is still correct.
When an agent writes CRUD::column('name'), it isn't searching or guessing. It already knows. Every rename you ship splits what the model learned into "old way" and "new way", and it will keep suggesting the old one for years.
There is a downside. Models sometimes write patterns from much older versions. We fix that with in-project instructions (more on that below), not by hoping the model catches up.
For your package: deprecate instead of rename. Keep old signatures working. Treat every breaking change as costing you twice: once for your users, once for every agent that learned the old API.
Our core, backpack/crud, is open source. That means ten years of GitHub issues, pull requests, tutorials, Stack Overflow answers and blog posts. All of it is training data. All of it is searchable when an agent does go looking.
You can't buy that. But if you're deciding between open source and closed, this is a new argument for open.
This is the one I think matters most for commercial packages. Composer installs everything into vendor/, including our paid add-ons. No obfuscation, no remote API. An agent can open the actual source of any feature, free or paid, and see exactly how it works.
We've always kept that code simple, commented and predictably organized, for humans. It turns out that's exactly what agents need too. In practice, reading vendor/ is how agents answer most of their own questions about Backpack. They do it without being told.
For your package: if you sell code, ship it readable. Obfuscated or SaaS-only features are invisible to the agent writing your customer's code.
Backpack has always been loose on purpose. You can override almost anything with a closure or a small tweak, without creating classes, registering providers or extending five things.
That turns out to be ideal for agents. Need a computed column? One line:
CRUD::column('full_name')->value(fn ($entry) => $entry->first_name.' '.$entry->last_name);
No custom column class, no view, no binding. Small changes stay in one file. That means less context for the agent to load, and fewer places for it to get things wrong. A strict, heavily abstracted architecture forces the agent to understand a lot before it can change a little.
For your package: for every extension point, ask how many files it takes to customize. If the answer is more than one, add a shortcut.
We added a Laravel Boost plugin for Backpack. Run php artisan boost:install, tick backpack/crud, and your agent gets our guidelines and skills straight in its context: which features exist, how to use them properly, which version-specific patterns to follow. The skill is split by topic (fields, columns, filters, operations, testing and so on), so the agent loads only the part it needs. We wrote about it when v7.1 shipped.
This worked where MCP didn't, for one reason: the agent doesn't have to decide to fetch it. It's already in context when the work starts. It also fixes the training-data downside above, because the instructions match the version actually installed.
For your package: if you're in the Laravel ecosystem, ship Boost guidelines. If you're not, ship the equivalent: a short, version-matched instructions file your users can drop into their agent's context.
php artisan backpack:crud Product creates the model, request, controller, route and menu item in one go. Then php artisan backpack:tests (from our backpack/test-generators add-on) writes a feature test for every CrudController, in PHPUnit or Pest, and backpack:tests:status shows which controllers still have no coverage. There are smaller ones too: backpack:field, backpack:column, backpack:filter, backpack:button, backpack:crud-operation.
This matters more with agents than without. A command gives the same correct result every time. Boilerplate the agent writes by hand is a fresh chance to make a small mistake in every file. The agent's time is better spent on what's actually specific to the project.
For your package: if users repeatedly write the same scaffolding, turn it into a command. Agents use CLI tools happily and reliably.
When names follow a pattern, agents guess right. A text field has a text column. A select2 field has a select2_multiple sibling, so select2_from_ajax has a select2_from_ajax_multiple one too. A date_picker field pairs with a date_picker column. The agent has seen one, so it correctly guesses the rest, without opening a single file.
Every inconsistency is a spot where the agent guesses wrong and you pay for it in review.
For your package: make things guessable. Same name for the same concept everywhere, same argument order, same patterns.
Our docs sit behind Cloudflare, and we turned on the feature that serves Markdown instead of HTML when an agent asks for it. Agents read our docs faster and with less noise. It's a small win, and a free one if you're already on Cloudflare.
In rough order of impact:
None of our biggest wins were clever. Stability, open code, simple architecture and good generators were all things we did for human developers. They just happen to be what AI agents need most too. The AI-specific additions only helped when they put the right information in front of the agent, without it having to ask.
One more thing, on the user side: use the best model you can get. The gap between today's frontier models and the ones on top six months ago is huge. It shows most on exactly this kind of work.
If you use Backpack with AI: how much faster are you building admin panels now? One hour instead of ten? A day instead of a week? Tell me in the comments. I'd love real numbers to compare against mine.
Subscribe to our "Article Digest". We'll send you a list of the new articles, every week, month or quarter - your choice.
What do you think about this?

articles.title: GIMP now has UI tests
articles.body:
GIMP has a lot of intertwined menus, dialogs and tools. When we change a part of the interface, another may stop working and sometimes, the problem can be missed until a user reports it.
To find these problems early, a new GUI testing platform was implemented. A typical GUI test starts GIMP, clicks menus and buttons, and then checks the result. These tests run automatically each time we merge contributor changes.
Why we need them
GIMP already has unit tests. A unit test checks one small part of the code, for example how GIMP reads an XCF file. But our unit tests were not opening a real window. So it coult not tell us if a dialog opens, or if a menu item did its job.
Note that GIMP already had tests of GUI code, usually interacting directly with the core code, and sometimes even simulating input devices’ events (pointer movements, clicks, drags…). But nothing can beat interacting with the real interface. Furthermore such legacy tests directly hijacking core code come with their own problems, such as breaking all too often (and not because they detected a bug), all while not being able to detect whole categories of bugs.
UI tests check the program as a whole, in the same way as you use it.
What the tests do
Each test starts a real GIMP and does one small task. Then it reads the result from GIMP. If the result is not correct, the test fails and tells us what went wrong.
We have 13 tests at this time. They check that:
- GIMP starts and shows its main window.
- The Welcome dialog opens on the correct tab. It also stays hidden when you turn off “Show on Start”.
- File > New makes an image with the size you set.
- File > Export As writes a correct PNG file.
- Tools > Swap Colors swaps the foreground and background colors.
- You can type a new foreground color in the Colors dialog.
- You can add a layer and delete a layer.
- Undo and Redo work.
- Zoom In changes the zoom level.
- A click on a tool button in the toolbox selects that tool. The test then uses the Bucket Fill tool on the canvas.
- A change in Preferences is saved when you click OK.
- A menu action, Image > Flatten Image, does its job.
How they work
The tests do not need a screen. Each test starts a small, hidden desktop, runs GIMP in it, and removes it at the end. Because of this, the tests can run on our CI servers, where no screen is available.
To find a button or a menu, the tests do not look at the pixels on the screen. They use the accessibility information that GIMP gives to tools such as screen readers. This has one more good result: when we make GIMP easier to test, we also make it easier to use with a screen reader, hence improve the software accessibility.
The tests use dogtail, a Python tool for UI tests. To run GIMP on a server with no screen, dogtail needed a new feature. We contributed this feature upstream, to dogtail itself, so other projects can use it too.
At this time, the tests run only on Linux (both X11 and Wayland) since
dogtail does not support Windows or macOs.
Adding even these few simple tests considerably increases confidence that the GIMP build has worked, and also shows the test infrastructure is working and useful.
Credits
- Harsh Verma wrote the UI tests and the new dogtail feature.
- Jehan reviewed the UI tests.
- Michal Odehnal reviewed the new dogtail feature.
You can read the full change in merge request !2909.
How you can help
13 tests is a good start, but GIMP has many more dialogs and tools. If you want to help, you can write a test for the part of GIMP that you use the most.
We wrote a guide that shows how to write a new test and how to find the cause when a test fails: UI tests on developer.gimp.org.
We hope this work will help us find bugs earlier and keep GIMP working well for everyone.
