articles.title: chocolate pecan pie bars
articles.body:
“Twenty years of Thanksgivings on Smitten Kitchen!” I told Ed Levine yesterday, as we chatted for an upcoming podcast episode [I’ll link it here as soon as it’s live], a statistic that remains baffling to me. What should one even have to show for two decades of Thanksgiving recipes, ideas, and advice? A degree in dry brining? A medal in single-oven-side-dish-rewarming Jenga? A metamorphosis into my final form: a human-shaped holiday cooking questions hotline (it’s me, or at least the texts on my phone)? Aspirationally, all of the above?
The only pattern I can identify in my Thanksgiving cooking evolution over the years is this: The more I’ve hosted, the more time I’ve spent having Real Talks (with myself, in my head) about what is actually worth my time, energy, and limited stove and oven real estate, the simpler — and I’d argue better — my recipes have become. Turkey? Dry-brined, with a gorgeous burnished finish and the best onions you’ll eat in your lifetime, all from six ingredients. Stuffing? Store-bought challah, celery, leeks, herbs, and a nobody-needs-to-know amount of butter. A carrot side dish? Start with one bag of baby carrots. Yes, really.
My pecan pie has gone through a few iterations over the years: first, a classic pecan pie (still a knockout, but it serves only eight, a travesty); then a chocolate pecan slab pie in my second cookbook, Smitten Kitchen Every Day (party-sized, hooray, but a serious time commitment, with two homemade crusts, a lattice, and a chocolate layer). A few years ago, I streamlined and simplified that recipe into these bars, and I haven’t looked back. The crust is pressed in. The topping is made in one bowl. Yet I’ve packed as much flavor as I possibly can into every bite: The pecans are toasted, there’s honey and dark brown sugar, vanilla bean, dark chocolate chips, sea salt, and there’s brown butter, both in the crust and the pecan layer. The aroma of the tiniest square leaps off the plate, and I think we should be there to catch it.
Pecan Pie Bars
- 1 cup plus 5 tablespoons (10.5 ounces or 300 grams) unsalted butter (to be used for crust and pecan layer)
- 2 tablespoons (30 ml) water
- 2 cups plus 2 tablespoons (275 grams) all-purpose flour
- 1/2 cup (60 to 100 grams) granulated or powdered sugar
- 1 teaspoon kosher salt (Diamond brand; use half of others)
- 2/3 cups (140 grams) packed dark brown sugar
- 1/2 cup (170 grams) honey
- 1/4 cup (60 ml) heavy cream
- 1/2 teaspoon flaky or coarse sea salt, plus an extra pinch or two to finish
- 1 teaspoon apple cider vinegar
- 1 teaspoon vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract
- 2 large eggs
- 3 1/4 cups (12 ounces or 340 grams) pecan halves, lightly toasted
- 1 cup (6 ounces or 170 grams) chocolate chips, semisweet or bittersweet are great here
Shortbread Crust
Pecan layer
[If your pecans aren’t already toasted, while the oven heats, place them on a sheet pan and bake them for 8 to 10 minutes, until fragrant. Set aside until needed.]
Brown the butter: In a medium-large saucepan (we’ll use this as the bowl to mix the pecan layer in a bit), melt butter over medium-high heat. It will melt, then foam, then begin to developed fragrant, toasted brown specks at the edges of the pan. Remove from heat when you see it starting to brown; the residual heat will be sufficient to toast the rest of the butter to a medium brown color. Carefully, so it doesn’t splatter, add 2 tablespoons of water.
Make the shortbread crust: In a large bowl, combine the flour, sugar, and salt. Measure 1 cup of the browned butter (leaving the rest in the saucepan) and add it to the flour mixture, stirring it until it’s mixed into a soft, crumbly dough. Scatter the dough over your prepared pan and press it evenly across the bottom and 1/4-inch further up at the edges. Transfer to the oven and bake for 15 to 17 minutes, until it smells fragrant and begins to get more golden at the edges.
Meanwhile, make the pecan layer: Add brown sugar, honey, heavy cream, flaky salt, cider vinegar, and vanilla to the remaining brown butter in your saucepan and whisk to combine. Add eggs, one at a time, whisking until fully mixed. Add your toasted pecan halves (still a little warm is fine) and stir to coat with honey mixture. Stir in chocolate chips last.
Assemble and bake: Pour the pecan mixture over the crust — it’s fine if it’s still hot from the oven — then sprinkle a few flakes of salt over the top. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, or until the edges are set but the center is somewhat firm to the touch, but still has some jiggle to it.
Transfer pan to a cooling rack and let the bars cool completely. You can hurry this along in the fridge. Use the edges of the parchment paper to lift bars out and onto a cutting board. Cut into your desired size pieces.
Do ahead: These bars keep in the fridge for up to a week, but only if you hide them from family and, sometimes, yourself.

articles.title: Rebuilding my local voice assistant pipeline
articles.body:
Rebuilding my voice assistant pipeline
Swapping openwakeword for microwakeword and making voice detection smarter
I wrote an article a couple of months ago describing how I rebuilt my old voice assistant pipeline in Platypush.
And I wrote earlier articles describing my journey through self-hosted voice assistants - in 2024 (with Picovoice), in 2020 (diving into the legacy assistant.google integration, the now defunct assistant.alexa integration, the now defunct Snowboy integration, the now defunct DeepSpeech integration and Picovoice) and the original article in 2019 describing the Google Assistant integration.
For a couple of months I used the voice pipeline described in my latest article as my main driver, but after getting used to the robustness of commercial voice assistants I was unhappy with the high rates of false positives/negatives of my self-hosted pipeline, as well as its lack of robustness in detecting start/end of speech, especially in noisy environments and using cheap microphones.
After a bit of experimentation, I decided to swap and fine tune a few parts, and after a couple of days of trying the results are satisfying enough for me to write a short article about it.
The resulting pipeline is:
Wake word detection: a new assistant.microwakeword plugin
Until recently I used assistant.openwakeword, which wraps openWakeWord.
It works, but the project has been quiet for a while and all of its pre-trained models are v0.1 files from 2023, mostly trained on synthetic speech.
In practice I was getting both false positives (the hotword triggering on background noise) and false negatives (the hotword not detected unless I was close to the microphone).
I added a new plugin, assistant.microwakeword, on top of microWakeWord through the pymicro-wakeword Python bindings.
microWakeWord is the engine used by ESPHome and Home Assistant Voice, its models are actively maintained, and the built-in models (okay_nabu, hey_jarvis, hey_mycroft, alexa) ship with the package — no download required.
The current official models are provided under the ESPHome micro-wake-word-models repository.
Custom models are supported too: drop a microWakeWord JSON manifest (with its .tflite model) in the plugin's models directory and reference it by name.
The plugin exposes the same API as assistant.openwakeword (same models, detection_threshold, frame_duration, patience_frames, input_device, input_volume parameters, same list_models action, same HotwordDetectedEvent), so switching is a matter of just changing the configuration to point to the new plugin:
assistant.microwakeword:
  models:
    - alexa
A few design notes:
- Without an explicit detection_threshold, each model uses the probability_cutoff from its own manifest (0.9 for alexa), which is the value the model was validated against.
- Models already smooth their output over a sliding window, so unlike openwakeword, patience_frames defaults to 0 here.
- The audio thread never touches the TFLite models directly: it queues frames (and a reset marker) to the main thread, because MicroWakeWord.reset() reloads the interpreter and isn't safe to call concurrently.
- Like assistant.openwakeword, the plugin releases the audio device when another assistant plugin starts a conversation, and re-acquires it when the conversation ends.
Speech-to-text: assistant.openai, with a much better ear
assistant.openai records audio when a conversation starts and transcribes it through Whisper.
The tricky part has always been end-of-speech detection: knowing when the user has finished talking. The previous implementation used a per-frame boolean from WebRTC VAD, and any single frame classified as speech would reset the silence timer. With even a bit of background noise, phrases would only end when the maximum conversation duration was hit.
The audio preprocessing layer (AudioPreprocessor, shared by the STT integrations) has been reworked:
- Silero VAD as the primary backend (through onnxruntime, no PyTorch required), with WebRTC VAD and a plain RMS-based detector as fallbacks. To get an idea of Silero VAD's performance compared against other solutions for speech activity detection, take a look at the insightful article One voice detector to rule them all. The Silero model is downloaded on first use into the Platypush workdir and checksum-verified:
assistant.openai:
  # auto = silero -> webrtc -> energy, depending on what's installed
  vad_backend: auto
- Hysteresis + sliding window: a frame becomes speech above the VAD threshold and stays speech until its score drops by a margin, and the per-frame decisions are smoothed by majority vote over a 0.5s window. A single noise burst can no longer keep a conversation alive.
- Adaptive noise floor: the background noise level is tracked over time, and frames that aren't louder than noise_floor_factor (default 2.0, ~6 dB) times the floor are never considered as speech.
On a synthetic benchmark (Piper-generated phrases mixed with babble and burst noise), the old settings kept conversations open for 6–10 seconds after the speech had ended; the new pipeline ends them 1.0–1.6 seconds after the last word, which is the configured conversation_end_timeout plus the smoothing lag.
Since the changes on Platypush have been performed directly in the AudioPreprocessor also used by other native speech-to-text engines, other speech-to-text plugins also benefit from them - e.g. if you use assistant.vosk for full on-device detection.
Responses and context: the openai plugin
The transcribed phrase is processed by the openai plugin, which handles both the API key and the conversation context. By default the assistant renders the response through the configured tts_plugin; if the response ends with a question mark, the conversation continues with a follow-up.
Custom hooks can intercept phrases before the default response kicks in — for example, to handle home automation commands locally without an LLM round-trip:
from platypush import run, when
from platypush.message.event.assistant import SpeechRecognizedEvent
@when(SpeechRecognizedEvent, phrase='play (the)? music')
def play_music():
    run('music.mpd.play')
And the hotword event is wired to the conversation start with a similar hook:
from platypush import run, when
from platypush.message.event.assistant import HotwordDetectedEvent
@when(HotwordDetectedEvent)
def on_hotword(**_):
    run('assistant.openai.start_conversation')
Text-to-speech: tts.openai
Responses are rendered by tts.openai, with volume and voice configurable. In my tests however tts.piper also yielded good results, and it runs entirely locally. In my tests on a RaspberryPi 5 however it added ~3-4s of latency to process the response to audio compared to tts.openai.
Since the TTS output goes to the speakers and the wake word detector listens on the microphone, the assistant plugins pause hotword detection while a conversation is active — otherwise the assistant would hear itself.
The full configuration
openai:
  api_key: YOUR_API_KEY
  # Or, for a custom setup using a model provider compatible with the OpenAI API,
  # e.g. a local Ollama instance:
  # base_url: http://localhost:8000/v1
  # model: gpt-5
  # Optional context that can be passed to initialize the assistant
  # context:
  #   role: system
  #   content: You are a useful assistant.
assistant.microwakeword:
  models:
    - alexa
assistant.openai:
  tts_plugin: tts.openai
  conversation_start_sound: ~/sounds/wake_word_detected.wav
  input_volume: 100
# assistant.vosk:
#   model: /path/to/vosk/model
#   conversation_start_sound: ~/sounds/wake_word_detected.wav
#   input_volume: 100
tts.openai:
  output_volume: 80.0
# Or, for a fully local setup that uses tts.piper:
# tts.piper:
#   output_volume: 80.0
What changed on the code side
- New assistant.microwakeword plugin: microWakeWord hotword detection through pymicro-wakeword, same API as assistant.openwakeword, built-in models bundled with the package, custom models via JSON manifests.
- assistant.openwakeword fixes: frames are now 80ms (1280 samples, the size openWakeWord recommends) instead of 500ms — longer chunks only return the highest score over their sub-frames and can miss hotwords — plus a patience_frames parameter (consecutive frames above threshold) and an explicit detection_threshold parameter (default 0.5).
- Shared AudioPreprocessor rework: Silero/WebRTC/energy VAD backends with vad_backend: auto selection, threshold hysteresis, sliding-window majority vote, and an adaptive noise floor. Used by both assistant.openai and assistant.vosk.
- New Silero VAD wrapper: ONNX inference through onnxruntime, recurrent state carried across frames, checksum-verified model download into the workdir.
Caveats
The microphone on my RPi doesn't support 16 kHz natively, so audio is captured at 44.1 kHz and software-resampled — it works, but if detection feels sluggish software resampling is usually the first suspect.
The VAD and threshold defaults were tuned on synthetic audio plus a couple of my audio recordings.
Different rooms, microphones and acoustics may yield different results. You may want to adjust detection_threshold on the wake word plugin and noise_floor_factor on the STT plugins if you don't feel satisfied with your mileage.

articles.title: Behind Jensen Huang’s exit, questions about a management style reportedly built on fear
articles.body:
Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”
Well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, and also by humiliating people.
According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate them with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him, and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.
Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

articles.title: A New Jean-Michel Basquiat Documentary Considers the Artist Behind the Work
articles.body:
A New Jean-Michel Basquiat Documentary Considers the Artist Behind the Work
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.
In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world.
As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

articles.title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
articles.body:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a now-removed job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which said Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.
Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.
“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing said. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”
With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.
Update, November 20th: Added that the job listing has since been removed.

articles.title: Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
articles.body:
Back in my day, the only “Doorbuster” sales were at physical retail stores. But now, you can get ultra-low prices before Black Friday whether you want to shop in-store or online. One that stands out is the previous-generation Sony WH-1000XM5 noise-canceling headphones, which are marked down to their lowest price ever, just $169.99 at Best Buy. While their MSRP is $399.99, they’ve been spotted as low as $198 in the last few months.
Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
Last-generation noise-cancelling headphones are still a great option for traveling or staying focused.
The WH-1000XM5 launched in 2022, and despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6, they’re still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones. There are some minor downsides, like a bulky case and all-plastic design, but those seem easier to overlook at this lower price point.
The newer Sony WH-1000XM6 improve the sound and noise cancellation, with quality of life upgrades not present in the XM5, like a folding design and more comfortable headband. However, they’re significantly more expensive, currently discounted to $348 during Black Friday (Amazon, Best Buy), down from their MSRP of $450.
To make shopping a little more confusing, the newer WH-1000XM4C sit between the XM5 and XM6 in terms of price, and are a slightly updated version of the older XM4 model with its foldable design. Our reviewer John Higgins thinks the XM4C’s noise cancellation lags behind, so I’d opt for the XM5 over them, especially at the sale price.

articles.title: Tubemap Mark Two: A geographically-accurate diagram of the London Underground
articles.body:
- Tube Map Mark Two A new version of the geographically-accurate diagram of the London Underground system
Tubemap Mark Two
A geographically-accurate diagram of the London Underground system
The New London Tubemap project is alternative look at mapping the London Underground system with the stations positioned so they are more geographically accurate in relation to each other. It is intended to help people, particularly those unfamiliar with the city, to relate the underground system to London at street level.
This second version, building on the original first published in 2011, anticipates the opening of the Elizabeth Line (formally known as Crossrail) and the extension to the Northern Line. An on-going project, this will continue to develop as indeed the network it represents will.
Purchase the Map
A pocket-sized version of the map
A2 folding to A6 – is available to buy from the Lettering Arts Trust shop. The price includes a donation to the charity.
A poster-sized version
of the original 2011 design is also available through the shop.
Origins
I think it’s safe to say that I never set out to redesign the London Underground map. The original design, conceived by Harry Beck in 1932, is a classic and one of the best pieces of graphic design of the 20th Century; I hold it in very high regard.
However, friends of mine from outside of London commented that they found the current map hard to use and in particular found the disconnect between the map and London at street level confusing.
This sparked my curiosity as a designer, would it be possible to design something as clear as the Beck map but manage to be more geographically accurate? That ‘thought experiment’ eventually expanded to become the complete alternative map of the system published in 2011.
With the imminent arrival of Crossrail (or the Elizabeth Line as it will be known), I thought it was time to update my map. Looking back at the design I published nearly ten years beforehand, I found I really didn’t like it very much any more. It’s a bit busy, a bit fussy in some places, slightly chaotic in others. One comment on the original was from writer and actor Mark Gatiss who described it as ‘aesthetically frightful’, and revisiting it, I think he has a point.
One of the hardest things to do as a designer is to put an idea to one side and come up with something different but that is what I did. Instead of just adding the new line to the old design, I rebuilt the whole thing from scratch. This time as well as the geographical parameter, I concentrated on making a simpler, more elegant solution adopting the 45º lines of the classic Beck original.
It is work in progress and will continue to change and develop as indeed the network it represents will continue to do. I have said all along that this is not intended to replace the standard map based on Beck’s original design, it’s simply another way of looking at it.
A note about the place name origins map
The version of the map showing the origins of the names of places on the London Underground system is a collaboration with writer Mark Forsyth www.inkyfool.com
This etymological guide is an updated and expanded version of The Etymological Map of the London Underground first published by Mark in 2011. It has now been expanded to include London Overground, the Croydon Tramlink, and the Elizabeth Line.

articles.body:
Gamers Skip Work to Play GTA VI After 13-Year Wait (nbcnews.com) 93
			
		 	
				After a 13-year wait, Rockstar games' Grand Theft Auto VI has officially (and finally) launched today to near-universal acclaim, earning a 99/100 score on Metacritic and generating an estimated $1.84 billion from 19 million copies sold. The highly anticipated release has prompted gamers to take time off work, attracted nearly 2 million concurrent Twitch viewers, and sparked celebrations around the world. "Video game critics have lauded it, describing it as a 'masterpiece' and 'the single most impressive video game' they've ever played," reports NBC News.
An expert told Reuters that there could be a "work blackout across the board." Another expert suggested that $1 billion in U.S. productivity could be lost as people take time off to play the game, which is estimated to take about 50 hours to complete.
Here's a roundup of GTA VI reviews:
-  IGN (10/10) calls it "the single most impressive video game I have ever played."
-  GameSpot (10/10) praises its extraordinary attention to detail, calling it a culmination of Rockstar's open-world achievements.
-  Push Square (10/10) describes it as Rockstar's deepest and most accomplished open world since Red Dead Redemption 2, though it notes the 30fps cap and occasional pacing issues.
-  Eurogamer (5/5) praises its ambitious world and the emotional depth of Jason and Lucia's relationship.
-  Digital Foundry highlights its groundbreaking visual realism, ray tracing, and simulation detail, while acknowledging compromises from the 30fps target.
-  Bloomberg calls it an all-time classic, praising the unpredictable interactions and remarkable freedom of exploration.

articles.title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
articles.body:
Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.
But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.
This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine, Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.
As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.
Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.
Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.
One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.
That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.
The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.
Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

articles.title: The Market Is Down
articles.body:
The market is down
Talk to anyone who has to work for a living and this is the common complaint you will hear atleast once in a conversation “the market is down”/”the market is bad” followed by fears of AI, job loss, increased prices and unaffordable homes. This conversation can be had without cultural and geographic barriers and across all age groups, more so with the young. Yet, Anthropic debuted with the best ever IPO worth over a trillion dollars yesterday. Technology that was meant to connect people and make our lives easier has slowly inched to the point of making copyrights and human labor irrelevant, focusing on an opaque chatbot do the work as one sits back and copy-pastes the output.
The entire nature of human survival has been reduced to precarity with the hopes that it remains this way or even becomes worse, because that's what a trillion dollar valuation for an AI company signals. A world where art isn't created for fun, where reading is relegated to information extraction and everything is a dashboard for pleasure or resource maximization. It's a time of great technological upheaval, yes, but makes one wonder how life was just 30 years ago when the chains of Wi-Fi and always on communications were still not delivered to the masses.
The market is down, but only for you and me. For the super-super rich, it's an upmarket time, a time of cheap slaves and plentiful labor. A world where our voice doesn't matter as much as long as they can hunker in their bunkers and slow drip us the promise of a capitalist salvation. And all of this alone, because who can plan for a family now? Children are the ultimate status symbol in this new world economy. With families successfully pulverized and the social contract broken, we sit alone trying to consume as little as possible for the incoming doom cycle to subside. The market is down and so are we.

If you find FFmpeg useful, you are welcome to contribute by donating. More downloading options
Get packages & executable files
FFmpeg only provides source code. Below are some links that provide it already compiled and ready to go.
Linux Packages
Linux Static Builds
Windows EXE Files
Get the Sources
You can retrieve the source code through Git by using the command:
git clone https://git.ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg.git ffmpeg
FFmpeg has always been a very experimental and developer-driven project. It is a key component in many multimedia projects and has new features added constantly. Development branch snapshots work really well 99% of the time so people are not afraid to use them.
Git Repositories
Since FFmpeg is developed with Git, multiple repositories from developers and groups of developers are available.
Release Verification
All FFmpeg releases are cryptographically signed with our public PGP key and should be verified for authenticity.
pub   rsa2048 2011-04-26 [SC]
    FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8
uid           [  full  ] FFmpeg release signing key <ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org>
sub   rsa2048 2011-04-26 [E]
  To verify a release:
- Import our public key into your local keyring:
        $ curl https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-devel.asc | gpg --import
- Download a release tarball and its corresponding signature.
- 
        Verify the signature:
        $ gpg --verify ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz.asc ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz gpg: Signature made Sun 21 Feb 2021 06:35:15 AEST gpg: using RSA key FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8 gpg: issuer "ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org" gpg: Good signature from "FFmpeg release signing key <ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org>" [full]
Optionally, you can verify that git and tarball match, the only differences should be the absence of .git* files in the tarball and a VERSION file in the tarball containing the version. The git tags should be signed with EDDSA key DD1EC9E8DE085C629B3E1846B18E8928B3948D64
    A release that also has a .pq.asc file carries post-quantum
    signatures (RFC 9980)
    made with both of these keys:
  
ML-DSA-87+Ed448  99669C49693683D51F174FE0D9E84915F5C2A536F5C0DA70FB8DCBD8AA8C4B3D
SLH-DSA-256s     547721479F80449E77748C0235116A1F8A73D9ECA98673B90E4E39347D229989
GnuPG cannot verify these yet; use sq 1.4 or later built with a cryptographic backend that supports these algorithms (OpenSSL 3.5 or RustCrypto), both of these must succeed:
$ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-mldsa87-ed448.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz
$ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-slhdsa256s.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz
Releases
Approximately every 6 months the FFmpeg project makes a new major release. Between major releases point releases will appear that add important bug fixes but no new features. Note that these releases are intended for distributors and system integrators. Users that wish to compile from source themselves are strongly encouraged to consider using the development branch (see above), this is the only version on which FFmpeg developers actively work. The release branches only cherry pick selected changes from the development branch, which therefore receives much more and much faster bug fixes such as additional features and security patches.

articles.title: You can now buy a Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist
articles.body:
Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.
You can now buy a Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist
Valve’s 512GB Steam Machine is available to buy now, but the 2TB model is out of stock.
The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. If Valve sells through its current inventory, the company says it will indicate that the product is out of stock instead of making another waitlist.
The bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve says there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The company is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.
Valve says that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The company anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.
After delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve launched the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

articles.title: Chrome AI features wasting much bandwidth
articles.body:
Chrome AI Features Wasting Much Bandwidth
🔎 Finally solved the mystery. At some point this year (around a few months ago), my bandwidth/data usage went thru the roof. Figured out it was Chrome’s recent AI features. Then got immediate bandwidth-relief after disabling all the “AI innovations” and “On-device” stuff. Here is a screenshot of the settings:
I simply disabled everything on that settings page, and the needless bandwidth leakage stopped immediately.
Don’t take my word for it. Fire up your favorite activity/network monitor. Watch the network activity while Chrome’s AI features are enabled, which they are by default. Note the continual bandwidth/data spend coming from Chrome, which if you care to monitor long-term adds up to many GBs per month (depending on setup, usage, etc.).
After watching the meter spin for a while, go into the Chrome settings and disable all the “AI innovations” and “On-device” stuff. Then return to the network monitor and watch it virtually flatline. Problem solved.
Commentary
Chrome should have left the AI resource hogs disabled by default. Someone do the math on how much energy and bandwidth is absolutely wasted by all the people (such as myself) who never touch the AI stuff.
Before I disabled the AI settings, Chrome was gobbling endless GBs. Multiply by the number of Chrome users who aren’t using “AI whatever neat”, and you’re talking real numbers. Real waste. For something that serves absolutely no purpose, that’s a ridiculous spend.
That’s all for now, I’m off to try some new browsers. There are quite a few great Chrome-alternatives these days.

articles.title: Palo Alto Networks Signs $4.5 Billion Deal For Applied Compute
articles.body:
Palo Alto Networks Signs $4.5 Billion Deal For Applied Compute 2
			
		 	
				Palo Alto Networks has agreed to acquire AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion as it expands beyond traditional cybersecurity into securing enterprise AI systems, including the training and deployment of open-weight models. The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027. Reuters reports:  Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi. The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks and gives attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities.
"AI tools are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than companies can patch them, and that is pushing customers to consolidate onto fewer platforms," said Catharine Trebnick, senior research analyst at Rosenblatt Securities. With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto aims to offer a technology platform that helps customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI.

articles.title: UK Government Forced To Disclose Secret Apple Backdoor Order
articles.body:
UK Government Forced To Disclose Secret Apple Backdoor Order (techcrunch.com) 6
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information. The Thursday ruling from the U.K.'s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret. The tribunal's ruling rejected the Home Office's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security. [...] A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year. The order follows a year-long dispute that began when British authorities reportedly sought a backdoor to users' data worldwide, drawing criticism from U.S. lawmakers over privacy concerns. Rather than comply, Apple disabled its Advanced Data Protection feature for U.K. users and challenged the order in court.
The government later narrowed its demand to British nationals' data, prompting another legal challenge from Apple.
Apple said it welcomes the ruling to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice, reiterating that it has "never built a backdoor or master key" to its products or services and "never will."

articles.title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
articles.body:
Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.
Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’
“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”
Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system.
Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.
“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

articles.title: Cornbread Salad
articles.body:
I love big community gatherings. Anytime there’s a melting pot of people, there’s bound to be really good food. I was born and raised in the South, and I love bringing this Southern-style Cornbread Salad to family reunions, church potlucks, holiday gatherings, and cookouts. It’s a hearty layered side with tender cubes of cornbread, pinto beans, crisp veggies, and sharp cheddar under a generous pour of homemade ranch (though you can add what you like!) It’s easy to make, packed with flavor, and at just $0.92 a serving, it might be the talk of the town at your next gathering!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
A Southern Potluck Favorite
This classic has been around for decades, and like so many recipes, it came out of necessity. Cornbread was often made in large batches, and sometimes the leftovers went into this colorful layered salad. And it still stretches your dollar today! A can of pinto beans, some budget-friendly frozen corn, and a few fresh veggies make this a hearty side that easily feeds ten. I rarely have leftover cornbread (because, well, cornbread), so I usually bake it fresh. For this salad, I adapted our everyday cornbread into a smaller loaf and kept the whole egg.
While the cornbread cools, I chop the veggies and stir together the ranch. I use plain yogurt and lemon juice in the dressing because their tang balances the lightly sweet cornbread. Once the bread is cool, all that’s left is to pile on the toppings and pour the ranch over the cheddar. You can even assemble the whole thing the day before, so the flavors have time to come together, and you have one less dish to make before everyone arrives!
Recipe Success Tips
- Mix the batter just until combined. When making the cornbread from scratch, I mix the dry ingredients together first so the baking powder is evenly distributed, then whisk the wet ingredients in a separate bowl. Once I bring the two together, I stop whisking as soon as the dry streaks disappear. Extra mixing can make the cornbread tough.
- Cool the cornbread completely before cubing. Warm cornbread is more likely to crumble under the knife. Once the loaf has cooled all the way through, the crumb firms up enough to cut into 1-inch cubes. Crumbled cornbread is still delicious here, but those larger pieces hold together better when you scoop through the layers.
- Rinse the beans and drain the corn well. Let the beans drain well in a colander and also pour off any extra liquid from the thawed corn. The less liquid that goes into the bowl, the less there is to soak into the cornbread and make the bottom layer soggy.
- Layering is pretty much up to you! I do recommend always starting with the cubed cornbread on the bottom so the other flavors can meld together. This salad is also typically topped with either the cheese or the dressing, so have fun!
how to make Cornbread Salad step-by-step photos
Gather all your ingredients: Preheat the oven to 425°F and lightly coat a glass loaf pan with nonstick cooking spray.
Mix the dry ingredients: In a medium bowl, stir together ½ cup cornmeal, ½ cup all-purpose flour, ⅛ cup sugar, ½ Tbsp baking powder, and ¼ tsp salt. Stir well so the baking powder is evenly distributed before you add the wet ingredients.
Whisk the wet ingredients: In a separate medium bowl, whisk together ½ cup milk, 1 egg, and ⅛ cup vegetable oil until you no longer see streaks of egg white.
Make the cornbread batter: Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and whisk just until the dry streaks disappear. A little graininess from the cornmeal is fine. I stop whisking here to keep the cornbread tender.
Pour the batter into the loaf pan: Scrape the batter into the prepared pan and gently spread it into the corners so it bakes in an even layer.
Bake and cool the cornbread: Bake for 20 minutes, or until the edges are golden brown and a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean. Set the loaf aside to cool completely before you assemble the salad.
Make the homemade ranch: While the cornbread cools, stir together 1 cup mayonnaise, 1 cup plain yogurt, 1 Tbsp lemon juice, ¾ tsp garlic powder, ½ tsp onion powder, 4 Tbsp chopped fresh parsley, 4 chopped green onions, ½ tsp salt, and ½ tsp pepper in a medium bowl. Stir until creamy and evenly flecked with herbs. Set aside the dressing and save the remaining 2 chopped green onions for the topping.
Chop the vegetables: Dice 1 green bell pepper, 1 red onion, and 3 Roma tomatoes into similar bite-sized pieces so they’re easy to scoop together. Keep them in separate piles on the cutting board so you can add each one as its own layer.
Cut the cornbread into cubes: Once the loaf is completely cool, cut it into 1-inch cubes. I like this size because the pieces are big enough to hold together when you scoop, but still easy to eat with a fork!
Start with the cornbread and bell pepper: Spread the cornbread cubes across the bottom of a trifle bowl, then scatter the diced green bell pepper evenly over the top. Bring the pepper right out to the sides of the bowl so that green layer shows through the glass.
Add the pinto beans and red onion: Rinse and thoroughly drain one 15.5 oz. can of pinto beans. Let the beans sit in the colander until they stop dripping so the extra liquid doesn’t soak into the bottom layer. Then spread them over the bell pepper and top with the diced red onion.
Layer on the corn and tomatoes: Drain off any extra liquid from 1½ cups thawed frozen corn and spread it over the red onion. Add the diced Roma tomatoes in an even layer.
Add the cheddar and ranch: Sprinkle 2 cups grated cheddar evenly over the tomatoes, then pour the homemade ranch over the cheese.
Finish with green onions: Sprinkle the remaining 2 chopped green onions over the ranch (I like to garnish with green onions, but fresh parsley, dill, basil, or chives would also be great). Serve and enjoy!
How to Serve Cornbread Salad
I always serve my cornbread salad in a clear trifle bowl so those colorful layers can be the centerpiece of the potluck table. A big serving bowl works just fine, too, or you can layer it in a glass baking dish with a lid if you’re taking it somewhere. For individual servings, try mason jars or clear cups. Set it out with a big spoon so everyone can scoop all the way down to the cornbread, or serve it alongside whatever you’re making for dinner.
If you’re making something that takes a little longer, like slow cooker pulled pork, you can assemble the salad while the pork cooks and pop it in the fridge until it’s time to eat. For a gathering or party, this salad is also right at home next to all the classic potluck favorites. The cool ranch and crisp veggies go so well with a hot scoop of cheesy potato casserole and a spoonful of sweet and tangy baked beans. Add a plate of deviled eggs, and you’ve got a spread worth a second trip to the table!
Storing Leftovers
Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a lid and refrigerate any leftovers for up to 2-3 days. The cornbread will soften as it soaks up some of the dressing and juices from the vegetables. I actually like the way the flavors come together overnight, but if you prefer firmer cubes, you can store the cornbread separately in an airtight container. You can also prep all the veggies and the ranch ahead, and store them separately until assembly, too. Drain the canned beans and any other canned add-ins well, and pour off any extra liquid from the thawed corn so it doesn’t pool at the bottom of the bowl before layering.
Freezing (just the cornbread!)
The assembled salad is best kept in the fridge since the vegetables can turn watery and the ranch can separate after thawing. To freeze the plain cornbread, let it cool completely, then wrap it tightly in portions and tuck them into a freezer bag or airtight container. Freeze for up to 3 months and thaw at room temperature before cutting it into cubes for the salad.
Try These Bean Salads Next:
- Like to get your potluck prep done early? Our Classic Three Bean Salad gets even better as the kidney beans, cannellini beans, and green beans soak up the sweet and tangy Dijon dressing.
- I’d bring this Cucumber and Black Bean Salad to a party with a bag of tortilla chips for scooping. The crisp cucumbers and tangy vinaigrette make it a refreshing side, too.
- A couple of cans of cannellini beans are the start of our easy White Bean Salad. Toss them with red onion, fresh parsley, and a lemon-Dijon vinaigrette for a side you can make in 15 minutes.

articles.title: 💧 Robots Are Ruining My Inbox
articles.body:
Believe it or not, there was a time when I found email to be a delight. Messages were infrequent, and there was an extremely high signal-to-noise ratio, with notes from friends, family, and businesses I cared about. Though spam grew to be a problem in the 2000s, paid spam filtering rapidly got quite good. The weekly chore of checking spam quarantines felt like an acceptable tradeoff for all the positives of email. Until very recently, nearly everything that reached my inbox was valid.
A.I., however, has shattered that peace. Every day, I’m now assailed with dozens of nonsense emails. These messages pitch me on reviewing new A.I-created software, taking out a line of credit, or hiring a company for a service I do not need, such as catering or dumpsters. It’s all very stupid, and I’m certain that A.I. has supercharged the problem.
It used to be that a relatively long, well-written email was probably worth a look, because it required effort to create. Now, however, A.I. can crap out a valid-looking message in seconds, and spend another few seconds scouring the web to gather targeted leads. The end result is that my spam filtering systems are getting overwhelmed.
Here’s a recent favorite, which I’ve lightly censored:
This is, of course, an utterly absurd request to make of a complete stranger. Even setting that aside, however, this is just so poorly done. I try to be generous, but Alexander No-Last-Name-Given didn’t give even the weakest of reasons why I might give him a gift. He also didn’t provide a location for this purported wedding, nor even mention his supposed spouse. Actually, the way the second sentence reads, it’s possible Alexander is intended to marry me. Won’t everyone be surprised when I fail to show?
I was amused when I first received this, and I’ve laughed several times as I shared it with others. Until I was writing this post, however, I was undecided as to the exact nature of the ploy. Is this a real-but-ridiculous request from a real dumb person, or is the entire thing a lie? I recently settled on the latter explanation, after checking next year’s calendar:
Yes, July 27, 2027 is a Tuesday. A Tuesday wedding! You’ve got to do better than that.

articles.title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
articles.body:
Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice. This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all, and has never really been.
Except in software engineering, somehow.
When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing. Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.”
Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all.
To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose!? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills.
“There’s more to software engineering than writing code” Link to heading
Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service!), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change.
Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you?
So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing!
Which brings me to my next point:
All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems Link to heading
if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems. And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it, then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error), and very few are learned without effort at all. Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window.
In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy, I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline, I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea.
It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all?
— Em’s blog2, emphasis mine.
Please, John Scofield, don’t stop playing your guitar!
- ↩︎
- I’m not sure who Em is, but their blog is great! ↩︎

articles.title: Carnival Cruises emits ten times more sulphur oxide than all of Europe's cars
articles.body:
In April, Ecohustler disrupted Carnival Cruise's AGM calling on the shareholders to reduce their company's pollution using straight forward and affordable methods - like burning cleaner fuel. Since then, a new report outlines the corporation's impact on the coastline of Europe. These vast floating cities are burning dirty bunker fuel and creating shocking levels of air pollution wherever they go. Shipping has been an unregulated industry for too long and action is urgently required.
Carnival Corporation, the world’s largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly 10 times more sulphur oxide (SOx) around European coasts than did all 260 million European cars in 2017, a new analysis by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals.
Royal Caribbean Cruises, the world’s second largest, is second, yet four times worse than the European car fleet. SOx emissions form sulphate (SO4) aerosols that increase human health risks and contribute to acidification in terrestrial and aquatic environments.
SUPPORTED BY HEROES LIKE YOU
Support independent eco journalism that drives real change.
In absolute terms, Spain, Italy and Greece, closely followed by France and Norway, are the European countries most exposed to SOx air pollution from cruise vessels while Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca and Venice are the most impacted European port cities, followed by Civitavecchia (Rome) and Southampton.
All photos by Greg English ©
These countries are so exposed because they are major tourist destinations, but also because they have less stringent marine sulphur fuel standards which allows cruise ships to burn the dirtiest most sulphurous fuel all along their coastlines.
Faig Abbasov, shipping policy manager at T&E, said: “Luxury cruise ships are floating cities powered by some of the dirtiest fuel possible. Cities are rightly banning dirty diesel cars but they’re giving a free pass to cruise companies that spew out toxic fumes that do immeasurable harm both to those on board and on nearby shores. This is unacceptable.“
NOX emissions from cruise ships in Europe also heavily impact some cities, equivalent to about 15% of the nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted by Europe’s passenger car fleet in a year, the report finds. In Marseille, for example, 57 cruise ships emitted in 2017 almost as much NOx as one-quarter of the city’s 340,000 passenger cars. Along the coasts of countries such as Norway, Denmark, Greece, Croatia and Malta a handful of cruise ships are also responsible for more NOx than the majority of their domestic car fleet.
Europe should implement a zero-emission port standard as soon as possible, this could then be extended to other ship types. The report also recommends extending emission control areas (ECAs), currently in place only in the North and Baltic Seas and English Channel, to the rest of the European seas. Furthermore, the report recommends regulating NOx emissions from existing ships, which are currently exempt from NOx standards applying in emission control areas.
Faig Abbasov concluded “There are enough mature technologies to clean up cruise ships. Shore-side electricity can help cut in-port emissions, batteries are a solution for shorter distances and hydrogen technology can power even the biggest cruise ships. The cruise sector are apparently not willing to make the shift voluntarily, so we need governments to step in and mandate zero emission standards.”

articles.title: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw
articles.body:
PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw 17
			
		 	
				PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across its supported versions, just four weeks after patches for the widely exploited PHP2Shell flaws. SecurityWeek reports:  One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines. PHP's maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code.
"An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled," PHP said last month. Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell.

articles.title: Google Will Launch Android App Verification Requirement Globally In January 2027
articles.body:
Google Will Launch Android App Verification Requirement Globally In January 2027 (arstechnica.com) 90
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon.
The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google's new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won't be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.
In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it's not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within "several months." So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with "millions" of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

articles.title: Leaked images reveal Motorola’s wide foldable
articles.body:
New leaked images of Motorola’s next folding smartphone shared by SammyGuru add more credence to the theory that widescreen could be the default design for foldables moving forward. Following a single leaked shot shared to Reddit yesterday, this new crop of images reveal the Motorola Razr Flex from several angles in two finishes with its inner screen completely open and partially folded.
Leaked images reveal Motorola’s wide foldable
The Razr Flex will compete with the iPhone Duo, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, and other widescreen folding devices.
The photos show the Razr Flex in two finishes: coriander brown and dark botanical garden, according to SammyGuru. The brown option features a back panel with a bumpy leather-like finish, while the green has a fabric-like woven finish. The cover screen has a hole-punch selfie camera centered at the top, while the Razr Flex’s inner screen pushes the camera to the upper right corner. On the back is a pill-shaped bar with two cameras and a flash.
The Flex is expected to be a smaller and more affordable alternative to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch main display when unfolded. But more specific details — including the size of the Razr Flex, its pricing, and when it’s expected to be debut — are still unknown.

articles.title: Apple’s iPhone camera leader has reportedly left the company
articles.body:
Jon McCormack, Apple’s vice president of camera software engineering, left the company last month, Bloomberg reports. Its sources say McCormack retired “at the end of October after more than eight years at the company.” Apple reportedly has not yet named a new VP to step in for McCormack, who oversaw its Camera and Photos apps, and the tech that defined generations of photos and the photography and editing experience on Apple’s devices.
Apple’s iPhone camera leader has reportedly left the company
Bloomberg reports Jon McCormack retired last month, continuing Apple’s recent leadership shuffle.
McCormack played a major role in defining how iPhone photos look, and he was always ready to get into the weeds with reporters after iPhone events. In 2024, he told The Verge that Apple sees a photo as “a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened.”
The departure follows John Ternus taking over for Tim Cook as Apple’s CEO in September. Apple has had other major leadership changes recently, including Phil Schiller stepping down as head of the App Store and Apple events and Steve Smith stepping in as the company’s new M&A and corporate development boss.

articles.title: Amazon is pushing alerts opposing NYC’s Delivery Protection Act
articles.body:
Amazon is serving up push notifications and banners on its home page to some users, warning that a new bill could add up to $5 per order in New York City. The Delivery Protection Act, which is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and a number of labor groups, including the Teamsters, would require Amazon to employ its current fleet of third-party delivery contractors directly.
Amazon is pushing alerts opposing NYC’s Delivery Protection Act
Amazon claims that a new bill could add $5 per order for New Yorkers.
Currently, Amazon turns to a network of small delivery companies and contract drivers to get its packages to your door. This is why your boxes are dropped off by a guy in a Toyota Camry sometimes, rather than an Amazon truck. The new bill would require that last-mile delivery firms be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers.
Next to Black Friday deal offers, now Amazon is showing a big tile with a red banner that says, “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Other users are reporting similar notices in the mobile app and after completing orders.
In a statement posted to its site, Amazon says that:
If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them [third-party delivery contractors], and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.
Mayor Mamdani and labor unions have countered that the current subcontractor model allows corporations like Amazon to avoid accountability and exploit vulnerable workers. In a statement to The Verge City Council Speaker Julie Menin said:
“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections. We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs. If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong.”
Mayor Mamdani responded on X, saying that if Jeff Bezos added $5 to your Amazon order, that’s just greed.
Amazon’s threats to leave New York to avoid regulation and efforts to unionize within the city follows shortly after the company’s third-quarter earnings report in which it said that it was on its way to having not one, but two trillion-dollar businesses in the next five to ten years.
Update November 19th: Added comment from Council Speaker Menin and clarification around licensing and Amazon’s delivery vehicles. Also embedded response from Mayor Mamdani.

articles.title: Let’s talk about GTA VI
articles.body:
It’s hard to believe, but Grand Theft Auto VI is now a real thing that we all can play. Thirteen years after GTA V, and eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar is back with its latest sprawling, extravagant open world. There’s a lot to experience — and a lot to talk about.
Let’s talk about GTA VI
The game is finally here, and there’s plenty to discuss.
Perhaps the most impressive thing about GTA VI is how flexible it is, letting you mold the experience to your own play style. You can still be a maniacal criminal, but you can also focus on the new love story that includes an entire button dedicated to holding hands. Or you can spend the hours fishing or driving around listening to the radio. Maybe you just want to doomscroll through a fake version of Instagram. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me just ahead of launch, “It’s a risk. It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”
Now that the game is out and people are finding their own way through Leonida, it’s a great time to start talking about it. I’ve played through the entire main story — you can read my review right here — but I’m nowhere close to experiencing everything in the game. But I’m happy to answer any questions you have, though I’ll be careful around some of the big story spoilers. I’ll also be joined by senior reporter Jay Peters, who is still early in the game and can offer a different perspective. There’s a good chance some other Verge staff will stop by as well, since we’re basically all playing it.
So drop all of your questions, theories, and stray thoughts about GTA VI here. I’ll be checking in throughout the day to join the conversation in the comments.
