articles.title: Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York
articles.body:
Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York
The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center, where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.
Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.
In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.
Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery, 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.
Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.
Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake. The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t.
In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb.
As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”
The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.

articles.title: Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite hasn’t been this cheap since June
articles.body:
Amazon debuted its latest Kindle Paperwhite in October, which is now available for $199.99 and replaces the outgoing 2024 model. However, given the minimal improvements on the new model — it’s a little thinner and opens books faster — the last-gen Paperwhite is still one of the best e-readers you can buy. And now, the latter is down to $129.99 ($70 off), nearly its lowest price ever, at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target.
Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite hasn’t been this cheap since June
At $129.99, it’s just $10 more than the base Kindle, only with a bunch of extra features.
Some important pricing context: The waterproof e-reader held steady at $159.99 until late August, when its price rose 25 percent due to rising component costs (many other Amazon tech products got more expensive, too). Even if the price hike never happened, though, this would still be a nice discount.
The $129.99 Paperwhite includes 16GB of storage and features lockscreen ads (it costs $20 extra to opt out at checkout), just like the newer version. It also packs a sharp 300ppi display with adjustable color temperature and USB-C charging. If you want more features — including twice the storage, zero ads, wireless charging, and an auto-adjusting front light — opt instead for the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition while it’s down to $179.99 (also $70 off), which is just $10 shy of its best price to date.
For the sake of being comprehensive, the last-gen base Kindle is going for $119.99 ($30 off) at Amazon ahead of Black Friday. While the standard Kindle has improved with each new iteration, it’s tough to recommend when the vastly superior Paperwhite is on sale for just $10 more. That 10 bucks gets you so much: waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher pixel density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches).

articles.title: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations
articles.body:
This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it.
- paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf: the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026).
- lean/: the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml).
  - lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2
and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper.
  - lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved.
The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in
place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/. Each
comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean, names the theorems whose statements must agree,
and permits only the axioms propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice.
To build, from lean/:
lake exe cache getlake build
The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time.
The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.
The source of the paper is not in this repository.
The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the
cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes
$(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$, one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics
of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the
conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.
